title: Direct monitoring of breaching in deltaic submarine landslides
source: Science
abstract: Submarine landslides threaten seabed infrastructure and trigger the transport of globally important amounts of sediment, carbon, and pollutants to deep-sea environments. However, fully submarine landslides have never been directly monitored in nature. Past hypotheses for their failure mechanism and dynamics therefore remain unvalidated for natural settings, including that prolonged upslope-migrating failures (breaching) occur in sandy seafloor environments. In this work, we present direct underwater monitoring of fully submarine landslides at Homathko Delta in western Canada that retrogress slowly upslope, indicating breaching-type failure. Their prolonged rather than instantaneous nature has important implications for the stress that seabed structures must be designed to withstand. Prolonged landslides also initiate sustained sediment flows (turbidity currents) that efficiently transport sediment, carbon, and pollutants further offshore.

title: Giant elastoresistance in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene
source: Science
abstract: Strongly correlated and topological phases in moiré materials are exquisitely sensitive to lattice geometry at both atomic and superlattice length scales. Twist angle, pressure, and strain directly modify the lattice and thus act as highly effective tuning parameters. Here, we examined electrical transport in twisted bilayer graphene subjected to continuous uniaxial strain. Near the magic angle (≈1.1°), devices exhibited a pronounced elastoresistance that depended on band filling and temperature, with a gauge factor more than two orders of magnitude larger than that of conventional metals. In selected doping regimes, the elastoresistance exhibited a Curie-Weiss–like temperature divergence. We discuss possible microscopic origins, including nematic fluctuations and enhanced electronic entropy from fluctuating isospin moments. Our work establishes uniaxial strain as a versatile probe of correlated physics in a moiré material.

title: A cellular atlas of the preinvasive breast cancer microenvironment
source: Science
abstract: Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is the most common preinvasive breast cancer, however our knowledge of the DCIS tumor microenvironment (TME) remains limited. We constructed a comprehensive atlas of the TME in estrogen-receptor positive DCIS using fresh samples collected from normal breast tissues, DCIS and invasive breast cancers. We analyzed 854,911 cells from 159 patients by single cell RNA sequencing and 39 samples by spatial transcriptomics, which identified 9 cell types and 60 cell states. Our data shows remodeling of fibroblasts, vascular and basal cells that encircle the DCIS regions and immunosuppressive ducts that support the growth of the preinvasive cancer cells. This study delineates early alterations in the DCIS TME, including many changes that persist during invasive progression.

title: The cryosphere beyond a planetary safe operating space
source: Science
abstract: The cryosphere plays a vital role in regulating planetary dynamics and habitability, yet it remains unclear whether its essential functions remain within a safe operating space (SOS) amid Anthropocene change. Here, we propose a cryosphere SOS and systematically evaluate its contributions to Earth system resilience using the planetary boundaries framework. Multiple lines of evidence indicate an accelerating and partly irreversible loss of cryospheric integrity, driven by amplifying feedbacks. Key cryospheric control variables either have left or are committed to departing from Holocene-like conditions. We conclude that the cryosphere has breached its SOS and is on a trajectory that locks in long-term risks for human societies and ecosystems. Safeguarding planetary resilience therefore requires explicit consideration of cryosphere change and its interactions across the Earth system.

title: Tracking danger on the peaks
source: Science
abstract: The Earth is warming, but not all regions are warming equally. In high mountain areas, temperatures are generally increasing by 1.5 to 2 times the global average, sometimes with devastating consequences. A small or gradual change in the mountain cryosphere—perhaps progressive thawing of frozen ground or a flood from a small glacial lake—can suddenly turn into a cascade of catastrophes with enormous ramifications. Monitoring systems for the cryosphere in high mountain areas have traditionally been designed to look at individual components and changes. What are the temperature and depth of the permafrost, or how much area is covered by snow, and what is the related avalanche danger? Many of the monitoring and warning systems were designed for historical patterns of snowfall or rainfall, and a river gauge may no longer be adequate if there is greater flow in the rainy season, or increased sediment that could damage the gauge.

title: Climate aridity amplifies global riverine nitrate beyond human inputs
source: Science
abstract: Nitrate pollution is widely perceived as a signature of human inputs. Here we show, with machine-learning reconstructed global maps, that climate aridity is also a dominant driver, systematically elevating nitrate concentrations across land-use gradients and creating unexpected hotspots beyond major agricultural and urban centers. Across ~2.9 million river segments worldwide, nitrate concentrations exceed ecological and health thresholds across ~33 and 2% of global land area, affecting ~5.6 billion (73%) and 0.5 billion (6%) people, respectively. Ecological threshold exceedance occurs mostly in headwaters, and about half of the health threshold exceedance occurs in middle-income countries and sparsely populated landscapes. These findings cast nitrate pollution as an aridity-amplified risk, suggesting that aridification may increase nitrate exposure even without additional human inputs. They call for regulatory standards that reflect risks across broad concentration ranges.

title: Phylogeographic and functional assembly of population-level bacterial immunity
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Bacterial pangenomes provide a shared reservoir of antiphage defenses, yet the ecological and functional constraints shaping this reservoir remain unclear. Here, we combine comparative genomics of 206 Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae (Xoo) genomes with cross-infection assays of 50 strains against 36 phages and heterologous expression of 24 defense systems in a phage-sensitive Xoo chassis. The Xoo pan-defensome comprises a conserved core of 9 subtypes and a variable layer of 35 accessory and cloud subtypes structured by host phylogeography. Phages are more infectious on sympatric than allopatric hosts, consistent with local adaptation. Variable systems show stronger apparent activity than core systems, whereas resistance breadth is not predicted by defense system number. Co-expression of representative co-occurring and mutually exclusive system pairs reveals synergistic and antagonistic interactions underlying non-random repertoire assembly. Together, these findings extend the pan-immunity framework by showing that population-level immune reservoirs are shaped by both ecological structure and functional compatibility.

title: A single NLS directs AGO1 import shaping small RNA loading and silencing outputs in Arabidopsis
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Small RNAs (sRNAs) regulate plant development, stress responses and genome stability by guiding ARGONAUTE (AGO) proteins to their targets. AGO1 is the major effector of microRNA (miRNA) and 21/22-nucleotide (nt) secondary small interfering RNA (siRNA) pathways in Arabidopsis thaliana. However, how AGO1 subcellular dynamics shape sRNA loading and silencing remained unclear. Here, we validate a functional nuclear localization signal (NLS) in the N-terminal extension of AGO1 and identify IMPORTIN α2 (IMPα2) as a nuclear import factor acting within a larger importin α network. Using engineered nuclear-only and cytoplasmic-only AGO1 variants, we show that exclusive cytoplasmic AGO1 allows full miRNA target repression and secondary siRNA production in ago1 mutants, whereas nuclear-retained AGO1 only partially rescues miRNA function and exerts a dominant-negative effect on secondary siRNA biogenesis. sRNA immunoprecipitation assay reveals that miRNAs are preferentially loaded into AGO1 in the nucleus, while tasiRNA loading predominantly occurs in the cytoplasm. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that AGO1 spatial partitioning itself quantitatively shapes the efficiency and specificity of sRNA loading and the silencing outputs.

title: A prefrontal microcircuit computes trial-wise discount of reinforcement during threat learning in male mice
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Threat learning requires rapid adaptation, but how the brain weights successive aversive experiences remains unclear. Here we show that many male mice exhibit delayed freezing acquisition during auditory fear conditioning. A trial-wise discount reinforcement learning model captured these dynamics through transient attenuation of early associative updating. Medial prefrontal neurons projecting to the periaqueductal gray constrained acquisition and subsequent cue-evoked freezing: inhibition increased freezing, whereas activation reduced it. Calcium imaging of individual neurons identified a subpopulation with delayed post-shock responses that declined during learning and predicted the model-derived discount-like variable. Temporally restricted inhibition implicated activity extending beyond the shock in constraining early acquisition. Local somatostatin interneurons showed increasing shock-evoked activity and provided inhibitory input to these projection neurons, suggesting a mechanism for relaxing this constraint. These findings link the trial-wise weighting of aversive experience to a prefrontal inhibitory microcircuit and provide a framework for understanding individual differences in threat memory formation.

title: Engineering CAR-Vδ2 T cells to boost persistence and anti-tumor function
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-modified Vδ2 T cells are an attractive therapeutic cell platform for cancer immunotherapy. However, their clinical efficacy is limited by short in vivo persistence due to insufficient cytokine support and high susceptibility to activation-induced cell death (AICD). Through comparison of membrane-bound (mb) cytokines, we identified mbIL-18 to support superior anti-tumor activity of CAR-Vδ2 T cells in vitro and in vivo. To reduce constitutive surface exposure of IL-18 and enable antigen-driven signal 3, we fused MyD88 - the key IL-18R signaling mediator - to an extracellular domain of Fas (Fas88). Antigen stimulation-induced FasL engagement of Fas88 triggered IL-18 signaling while simultaneously protecting Vδ2 T cells from AICD. Fas88-armed human CAR-Vδ2 T cells produced superior yet stimulation-dependent in vivo expansion and functional persistence in xenograft models of hematologic and solid malignancies. Together, these findings highlight the importance of IL-18 signaling and AICD resistance for CAR-Vδ2 T cell activity, enabling a single-transgene modification to limit inflammatory risk and facilitate clinical translation.

title: Epigenetic gatekeeping enables genome-scale horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotic cells
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Horizontal gene transfer drives rapid evolutionary innovation, yet well-substantiated cases are largely confined to prokaryotes. Eukaryote-to-eukaryote transfer remains exceptionally rare, and direct genome-scale demonstrations are absent. Here, inspired by endosymbiotic genome acquisition, we show that mammalian cells can initiate genome-scale horizontal gene transfer through phagocytic uptake of intact algal cells, albeit at a much lower frequency than cell fusion. Live-cell imaging captures the early nuclear appearance of transferred algal DNA after fusion, while genome sequencing and cytogenetic analyses reveal stable retention of chromosome-scale algal DNA in mammalian cells. Hybrid cells maintain more than 16 Mb of algal DNA, including intact chromosomes, as telomere-linked structures that persist for 95 generations without selection. Transferred algal DNA shows a progressive increase in DNA methylation together with enrichment of repressive histone modifications, forming heterochromatic domains that physically associate with host chromosomes. Notably, mammalian cells deficient in a de novo DNA methyltransferase show reduced stable establishment and retention of transferred algal DNA, supporting a gatekeeping role for DNA methylation in the stable accommodation of foreign genomes. Our findings reveal an epigenetic mechanism that contributes to the stable accommodation of large-scale foreign DNA between distantly related eukaryotes.

title: Anion Sublattice Engineering Induced Niobium-Tungsten Oxide with Near-Zero Residual Strain for Stable 100 C Cycling Capability
source: ACS Energy Letters: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Wadsley-Roth W3Nb14O44 is a fast-charging anode material but suffers from low electronic conductivity and electrochemical polarization. Here, anion-sublattice engineering is employed to regulate its electronic structure and Li+ storage kinetics. Density functional theory and kinetic analyses reveal that an appropriate concentration of oxygen vacancies enhances electronic conductivity, moderates Li+ adsorption, and facilitates Li+ diffusion, thereby reducing charge-transfer and diffusion impedances at low temperatures. In situ XRD and synchrotron radiation X-ray 3D nanocomputed tomography reveal reversible structural evolution with near-zero residual strain after cycling. Consequently, WNO-x delivers 77.4 mAh g–1 at 200 C and retains 72.6% capacity after 6000 cycles at 100 C while exhibiting low-temperature electrochemical activity. Moreover, the WNO-x||LiNi0.8Co0.1Mn0.1O2 full cell delivers 85.8 mAh g–1 at 20 C and retains 77.1% capacity after 3000 cycles, with cycling capability at –30 °C. Such structure-property insight provides a strategy for designing niobium-based oxide anodes toward fast-charging and low-temperature batteries.

title: Constructing exclusive Pt@WOx interfacial sites enables selective C–O bond activation
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Precisely constructing exclusive metal-oxide interfacial active sites while eliminating non-interfacial species represents a longstanding challenge in heterogeneous catalysis. Here we construct catalysts featuring exclusively isolated Pt@WOx interfacial sites via a controlled electrostatic adsorption strategy, thereby eliminating non-interfacial Pt species, enabling controlled reaction pathways. We identify that selective C–O bond activation is governed by the availability of interfacial reactive hydrogen, where isolated Pt sites drive deep hydrogenolysis, while Pt@WOx interfacial sites control reaction pathways by constrained hydrogen availability. This principle is validated in glycerol hydrogenolysis, achieving a high 1,3-PDO selectivity of 73.5% at a low temperature of 130 °C. Experiments reveal that 1,3-PDO selectivity is not enhanced by increasing active site density, but by eliminating intrinsically unselective sites, thereby reshaping the reaction energy landscape to suppress thermodynamically driven over-hydrogenolysis. This architecture provides an ideal platform for disentangling interface effects from contributions arising from non-interfacial metal species.

title: Comparative investigation of temperature-dependent defect evolution and irradiation hardening in CVD and ITER-like tungsten
source: Nuclear Fusion - latest papers
abstract: Chemical vapor deposited tungsten (CVD-W) is known for its high thermal stability of the microstructure and lower susceptibility to deuterium-induced blistering compared to ITER-like W (IL-W). However, it remains unclear whether these advantages extend to displacement damage tolerance. To address this, CVD-W and ITER-like tungsten (IL-W) were irradiated with 6 MeV copper ions up to 0.6 dpa at room temperature (RT), 773 K, and 973 K. Transmission electron microscopy, defect statistics, and nano-indentation revealed comparable damage accumulation and irradiation hardening in both materials across all investigated temperatures. At RT, both materials exhibited dense dislocation networks and loops, together with very sparsely distributed voids, resulting in comparable increases in hardness. At elevated temperatures, these networks disappeared, giving way to dislocation loop strings and dislocation lines, along with an increased density of voids, accompanied by further irradiation hardening. The dispersed barrier hardening model analysis indicates that the dominant contribution to irradiation hardening transitions from dislocation structures at RT to voids at elevated temperatures. In addition, differences in dislocation morphology and nature were observed between the two materials. Displacement damage defects in CVD-W exhibited higher mobility than in IL-W, as evidenced by an expanded damage layer, a higher degree of dislocation loop ordering into one-dimensional strings, a larger fraction of glissile 1/2 dislocation loops, and a greater proportion of loops exceeding 10 nm at ⩾773 K, mainly owing to its lower impurity content. This further supports void-dominated hardening at elevated temperatures, as different dislocation morphologies observed at elevated temperatures had minimal impact on the overall hardening. These findings provide valuable insights into the irradiation response of CVD-W under fusion-relevant conditions.

title: First observation and interpretation of ion cyclotron emission from energetic ions accelerated by lower hybrid waves in a tokamak plasma
source: Nuclear Fusion - latest papers
abstract: We report the first observation of ion cyclotron emission (ICE) from a tokamak plasma during lower hybrid wave (LHW) injection and electron cyclotron resonance heating. Using a novel approach derived from linear kinetic theory, we infer key parameter values for the LHW-accelerated fast-ion distribution which drives the observed ICE spectra, and for the bulk plasma. These ICE spectra from deuterium plasmas in the EAST tokamak exhibit peaks at successive deuterium cyclotron harmonics, consistent with the collective relaxation of energetic deuterons through the magnetosonic cyclotron instability (MCI). By carrying out a multi-dimensional parameter scan of MCI growth rates in high-resolution two-dimensional ( ) wavenumber space, we obtain best-fit values for: the magnetic field; plasma density; background electron and ion temperature; and the concentration of fast deuterons, together with their energy, pitch ( ) and thermal spread. We find that the observed ICE spectrum is likely driven by 770 keV deuterons, plausibly accelerated through LHW–ion interactions, which then undergo the MCI. The assumptions of the linear analytically based model include an infinite homogeneous plasma, and a ring-beam distribution of fast deuterons. Our results demonstrate a new scenario in which ICE serves as a passive diagnostic of energetic ion populations, and invite further investigation of the ICE–LHW connection.

title: Structural basis of ligand-mediated transition to higher-order rubisco assemblies
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Proteins often assemble as higher order complexes, underlying a diversity of molecular structures and biological functions. The emergence of protein-protein interactions between binding partners is generally considered to be the primary driver of oligomerization. However, ligand binding has also been demonstrated to affect higher-order assembly, though this phenomenon is not widely considered as a primary driver of oligomerization. Here, we describe the mechanism by which different rubisco oligomeric states are induced via ligand binding. By expanding the phylogenetic sampling of a unique clade of rubisco, we discover a range of oligomeric responses to ligand binding across the phylogeny and identify the structural features responsible for shifts in the oligomeric state that ultimately provide a path to evolving new quaternary structures. Here, we identify a ligand-dependent mechanism giving rise to new protein assemblies, in contrast with the typical process of evolving new protein-protein interfaces directly. Our findings describe a means by which binding and entrenchment of a ligand enables an increase in structural complexity.

title: Six-dimensional programmable ultrasonic vibration for multimodal object manipulation
source: National Science Review Advance Access
abstract: Object manipulation via external stimuli is a pivotal technology across physics, engineering, and materials science. However, the strict material requirements and complex manipulation systems of existing approaches limit the operational flexibility, functional versatility, and material adaptability. Here we present an approach for generating six-dimensional (6D) programmable ultrasonic vibration. The 6D vibration consists of three-dimensional (3D) translational vibration and 3D rotational vibration, generated through coupling and superposing of multiple longitudinal and bending vibration modes. Selective spatiotemporal combination of these vibration components enables the construction of programmable vibration fields. Most importantly, we realize multimodal manipulation of individual and collective objects positioned on a 6D vibrating surface, including trapping, translation, rotation, bounce, and reconfiguration. We demonstrate highly adaptive manipulation of objects with various shapes, materials, and scales. Furthermore, diverse applications are conducted at both the macroscale and microscale. This work opens avenues for the development of ultrasound manipulation.

title: The Iberian blackout: A black swan or a gray rhino? A protection-aware dynamic voltage security assessment
source: ScienceDirect Publication: Applied Energy
abstract: On 28 April 2025, the Iberian power system collapsed after a rapid voltage rise that led to widespread generation disconnections and loss of synchronism. The final report of the ENTSO-E Expert Panel attributes the blackout to several interacting factors including ineffective voltage control, fixed power factor operation, misaligned protection settings, manual shunt reactor switching, and limited observability. These factors raise a general question: given the current state, can the next trip, ramp, topology action, or shunt switching raise the voltages measured by overvoltage relays above their settings before voltage controls respond? We answer this with a protection-aware dynamic voltage security assessment. For each candidate event, the method computes the voltage at every overvoltage relay over the relay time window from a dynamic model of the network, its controls, and its relays. It predicts which relays trip after a first trip, identifies assets whose relay or measurement data are insufficient for a safety conclusion, and, when one exists, computes a minimum-cost fast reactive power action that keeps all relay voltages below their settings. Case studies on four benchmark systems and a 2000-bus system that reproduces the mechanism of the Iberian blackout show that the method flagged every event that caused a secondary trip within the relay window, never declared safe a plant that tripped within that window, and, on the benchmarks, found fast reactive power actions that prevented the trips within the relay window whenever it judged such actions feasible. These results were validated with nonlinear time-domain simulations. The implementation code and a visual guide of this work are publicly available.

title: scMomer: a pretraining framework for inferring robust cellular representations from single-cell transcriptomes
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: High-quality cellular representations are important for understanding complex biological systems. However, due to limitations in both data availability and practical utility, most existing computational methods are designed for a single modality (e.g., scRNA-seq or scATAC-seq), restricting their ability to capture cellular heterogeneity. Here, we propose scMomer, a multistage pretraining framework designed to infer robust cellular representations by integrating multimodal knowledge into scRNA-seq-only inputs. The framework progressively learns through three stages. Firstly, it pretrains unimodal encoders on single-modality datasets to obtain modality-specific representations. Secondly, it aligns these modalities using paired data to learn joint representations. Thirdly, it applies knowledge distillation to transfer knowledge of the missing modality (scATAC-seq) into a cross-modal student encoder, enabling the inference of multimodal-aware representations from scRNA-seq-only inputs. We perform extensive experiments show that the representations learned by scMomer achieve superior performance compared with state-of-the-art methods across diverse tasks, including cross-modality translation, cell annotation, drug response prediction, perturbation prediction, and gene property prediction, demonstrating its robustness and versatility. Overall, we demonstrate that scMomer enables unimodal data to yield robust cellular representations, providing an effective solution to missing-modality modeling.

title: ISG15 promotes PARP inhibitor resistance in BRCA1-deficient cells by facilitating DNA replication and repair
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: The use of poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPi) has proven largely successful in targeting BRCA1/2-mutated tumours. However, the emergence of PARPi-resistant disease can reduce the efficacy of this treatment, posing significant challenges in the clinic. Here, we use multiple models of BRCA1-/- cells and patient-derived xenografts (PDXs) that have been treated with PARPi until they no longer responded to the drug, to characterise genomic and transcriptomic alterations specific to PARPi resistance. We find that abrogation of TP53BP1 expression occurs spontaneously during prolonged PARPi treatment, alongside TP53BP1 genomic deletions and promoter methylation. Additionally, innate immune response genes, including ISG15 and factors of the ISGylation machinery are upregulated in PARPi-resistant cells and tumours. We demonstrate that ISG15 inhibition re-sensitises PARPi-resistant cells to the drug and, conversely, that ISG15 overexpression in BRCA1-/- cells promotes PARPi resistance. Mechanistically, BRCA1-/- PARPi-resistant cells rely on ISG15 for replication fork progression and restart of stalled forks and for DNA double-strand break (DSB) repair via homologous recombination (HR). Our results indicate that complex ISG15 interactions with DNA replication/repair factors can drive PARPi resistance in BRCA1-deficient cancer cells and that targeting ISG15 has the potential to overcome PARPi resistance.

title: Extinction risks in deep-sea populations revealed by genomic data and ecological niche modeling
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: As the global biodiversity crisis accelerates across terrestrial and shallow marine systems, the extent of this collapse remains unknown within the deep sea. Despite encompassing most of the ocean, deep-sea ecosystems remain the planet’s final frontier. Within this vast realm, the mesopelagic zone represents a critical yet poorly understood habitat, particularly in terms of its conservation status. Here, we integrate genomic data with ecological niche modeling to assess and forecast the conservation status of five mesopelagic species in the Gulf of Mexico. Samples were collected from 2011 to 2023, representing one of the longest time-series datasets for mesopelagic fauna in oceanographic history. All species exhibit current effective population sizes below the minimum thresholds for long-term viability. Genomic diversity declined over a decade in some species at rates comparable to or exceeding those reported for threatened and endangered species. Demographic modeling indicates historical population declines across all species. Ecological niche models predict declining Gulf habitat suitability for most species under future climate change scenarios. Together, our results identify indicators associated with elevated extinction risk in Gulf mesopelagic species and raise the possibility of a broader, unnoticed crisis, challenging assumptions of stability and resilience in mesopelagic ecosystems.

title: ESCRT-0 condensation and cargo clustering drive extracellular vesicle budding from cilia
source: Science
abstract: Cilia-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) mediate cell-cell communication and remove signaling molecules from cilia. The Hedgehog receptor Smoothened (SMO) is selected for packaging into ciliary EVs by ubiquitin chains, but how cargo selection is coupled to EV budding remains unknown. In this work, working in mouse kidney cells, we found that the ubiquitin reader endosomal sorting complex required for transport–0 (ESCRT-0) orchestrates both cargo selection and EV biogenesis. Unlike the conventional ESCRT pathway, SMO secretion did not require the ESCRT-III membrane scission machinery. Instead, ESCRT-0 condensed at the ciliary tip, where it clustered ubiquitinated SMO to drive EV biogenesis. Disrupting ESCRT-0 condensation blocked SMO secretion, and combining forced recruitment of ESCRT-0 with optogenetic clustering of SMO was sufficient to reconstitute EV budding. Thus, ESCRT-0 condensation and cargo clustering constitute a minimal module for ESCRT-III–independent reverse-topology budding.

title: Early epidemiological and spatial assessment of the Bundibugyo virus outbreak 2026
source: Science
abstract: A Bundibugyo virus outbreak was first reported on May 15th, 2026 in Ituri province, Democratic Republic of the Congo, with multiple cases reported across health zones during the early phase of the outbreak and suggestions of circulation weeks prior to detection. We pair highly resolved case and testing records with human mobility data to investigate the early outbreak dynamics of Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD). We show that human movement was a principle driver of early spatial expansion between May 10th and June 1st when the number of health zones and health areas reporting positive cases increased by 12 and 49, respectively. The early doubling time was estimated at ~10 days. Our work shows the rapid spatial expansion and growth of BVD with implications for intervention strategies.

title: Geodetic observations in West Antarctica reveal geodynamically consistent 3D mantle viscosity
source: Science
abstract: The rapid ice loss in West Antarctica since the 1990s has led to substantial ice surface lowering, regional bedrock uplift, and gravity reduction, as measured by geodetic observations. The bedrock (crustal) motions and gravity changes result from glacial isostatic adjustment (GIA), a process controlled by Earth’s viscoelastic properties and deglaciation history. In this study, we present GIA models with geodynamically consistent three-dimensional mantle viscoelastic structures and reconstructed ice history for Antarctica from 1900 to 2020, which explain both the observed Global Navigation Satellite System crustal motions and Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment gravity changes in West Antarctica. This study demonstrates that a mantle rheology including a weak asthenosphere and temperature-dependent viscosity is consistent with both mantle convection at million-year timescales and ongoing decadal GIA occurring in West Antarctica.

title: Alkali-Assisted MOCVD Growth of Polycrystalline MoS2 with Micrometer-Scale Domains on Soda-Lime Glass
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Achieving large-scale, uniform MoS2 films with reduced grain boundary density remains a central challenge for scalable device applications. Previous studies have reported that alkali-assisted growth promotes lateral domain expansion through eutectic intermediate formation. Here, metal–organic chemical vapor deposition (MOCVD) of MoS2 on commercial soda-lime glass is investigated. The intrinsic alkali content of soda-lime glass provides a uniform supply across the substrate, while partial surface softening at growth temperature facilitates the incorporation of Mo species within the near-surface region of the glass. The systematic variation of precursor flow conditions enables controlled modulation of nucleation density and domain size while suppressing graphitic carbon co-deposition arising from precursor ligand pyrolysis. High-quality polycrystalline MoS2 with lateral grain sizes ranging from ∼500 nm to 1.5 μm is achieved as uniform, coalesced centimeter-scale films, demonstrating the scalability of this method. Substrate roughness and wafer-to-wafer variability are key factors governing nucleation, highlighting opportunities for substrate optimization. To correlate the material properties with device performance, the films are wet-transferred and integrated into bottom-gated, top-contact field-effect transistors featuring either non-interdigitated or interdigitated source-drain electrodes. The devices exhibit on/off current ratios up to ∼107 and mobilities of ∼8 cm2 V–1 s–1. Overall, this work demonstrates an accessible and scalable route for the growth of electronic-grade polycrystalline MoS2 on soda-lime glass substrates.

title: Cobalt based anode for highly stable alkaline water electrolysis under operation conditions beyond industrial requirements
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Alkaline water electrolysis is the most established route to electrochemical hydrogen production, but the limited lifetime of anode catalysts makes long-term equipment investment costly and hinders miniaturization. Here we show that, unlike the extensively investigated nickel- and nickel–iron-based hydroxides, the long-neglected cobalt–nickel hydroxides are promising anode catalysts whose stability exceeds current industrial requirements. A cobalt–nickel layered double hydroxide anode enables stable alkaline water electrolysis for more than 8,000 hours at 1 A cm–2 in 6 M sodium hydroxide at 80 °C. This stability arises from the strengthened metal–oxygen bonding of the in-situ-formed cobalt–nickel oxyhydroxide, which raises the energy barrier for lattice-oxygen loss during the oxygen evolution reaction. In a practical electrolyzer, the anode achieves an energy consumption of ~4.2 kWh per normal cubic metre of hydrogen at 1 A cm–2 and operates stably for thousands of hours. The design of high-current-density alkaline electrolyzers should therefore prioritize robust anode stability under industrial conditions in addition to activity optimization.

title: Emergent stoichiometric host-guest recognition on ligated colloidal surfaces via dynamic ligand reorientation
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Physical adsorption on ligand-protected colloidal nanoparticles is central to their properties and applications, yet adsorption events on dynamic ligand shells are rarely defined, counted, or quantified with molecular precision. Here we show that on a native ligand shell without pre-designed receptor-like motifs, molecular adsorption can trigger stoichiometric host-guest recognition through dynamic ligand reorientation. In aqueous dispersion, atomically precise [Au25(p-MBA)18]− (p-MBA = para-mercaptobenzoic acid) nanoclusters accommodate tetraalkylammonium ions within transient aromatic pockets formed by three to four neighboring p-MBA ligands. NMR titration and diffusion-ordered spectroscopy reveal an apparent saturated binding number of six guests per nanocluster, with an apparent association constant of ~3.5 × 104 M−1 and ΔG of ~−25 kJ•mol−1 for tetrapropylammonium binding. Molecular simulations and free-energy analysis rationalize this stoichiometry through a cooperative yet self-limiting mechanism, in which ligand reorientation creates bowl-like pockets stabilized by multiple CH···π interactions while steric constraints limit further guest accommodation. The guest-size- and surface-dependent binding behaviors further reveal the adaptive nature of emergent pockets. These findings change the role of the ligand shell from a stabilizing layer or diffuse adsorption medium to an active supramolecular interface capable of producing molecularly defined recognition, paving the way for adaptive nanomaterials, selective sensing, and stimuli-responsive colloidal systems.

title: Autapse-inspired neuromorphic hardware with synapse–neuron integration for bidirectional feedback control
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Establishing autonomous and energy-efficient feedback control at the hardware level remains challenging because conventional systems rely on centralized processing and continuous external computation, increasing energy consumption and system complexity. Here we show a neuromorphic autapse-inspired system that enables localized and bidirectional feedback control, using thermoregulation as a representative application. An autapse is a self-synaptic connection in which a neuron feeds its output back to its own synaptic input, enabling intrinsic feedback modulation. The system integrates a solid electrolyte-based synaptic transistor capable of multiplexing multiple inputs and a bidirectional leaky integrate-and-fire artificial neuron. By feeding the neuronal output back to an additional synaptic gate, excitatory and inhibitory feedback loops are realized within a compact architecture. Using an artificial thermoregulation platform, temperature-dependent inputs bidirectionally modulate neuronal firing frequency, demonstrating biologically inspired feedback control with a compact set of neuromorphic devices for autonomous and energy-efficient systems.

title: Thin-film lithium niobate waveguide-integrated p-i-n Tungsten selenide photodiodes with 10Gbit/s data reception
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) is a promising photonic platform in next-generation integrated optoelectronics and on-chip/chip-chip interconnection due to its attractive optical property and versatility. However, integration of conventional-material-based photodetectors on TFLN platforms still faces multiple challenges. Herein, a high-bandwidth TFLN-based waveguide-integrated lateral WSe2 p-i-n photodetector is presented. The localized self-aligned doping process eliminates slow carrier diffusion and defect trapping in doped regions which further boosts modulation bandwidth. Secondly, n-type and p-type Ohmic contacts, along with a high-quality p-n junction, are achieved through Se vacancy defect engineering and high-work function molybdenum oxide buffer layer, respectively. Furthermore, combined with the high dielectric constant of lithium niobate suppressing ionized impurity scattering, carrier mobilities exceeding 350 cm2/V·s are achieved for both electrons and holes, significantly accelerating carrier drift. The device features a measured bandwidth of 1.12 GHz and a data rate up to 10 Gbit/s in visible light. Separately, the device achieves a responsivity of ~492 mA·W−1 and a near-unity external quantum efficiency of 95.6% at 638 nm. This combination of two-dimensional homostructure and TFLN nano-waveguides provides a basis for high-speed photodetectors and visible-light interconnections in future TFLN integrated optoelectronics and optical input/output applications.

title: Latitude modulates climate-driven maize yield gains across the central U.S. “warming hole”
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Maize yield responses to climate change differ seasonally and regionally, with both positive and negative impacts shaped by local climate trends and management decisions. Here, using a phenology-aligned moving crop-season framework and the Hybrid-Maize model (1991–2024) across five U.S. Corn Belt states, we quantify climate-driven yield contributions and show that they transition from southern declines to northern gains, reflecting the persistent influence of the central U.S. summer warming hole characterized by cooling maximum temperatures and increasing rainfall. A systematic thermal mismatch between environmental heat availability and hybrid growing degree day requirements is observed, particularly south of 42°N, where thermal matching declined despite favorable thermal conditions. Contrasting trends in thermal matching and reproductive duration help explain the latitude-dependent structure of climate-driven yield contributions. Our findings highlight how hybrid selection modulates the impacts of temperature, precipitation, vapor pressure deficit, and radiation trends on maize yield gains across the U.S. Corn Belt.

title: Evolution of the molybdenum and vanadium cycles through time and their impact on ancient nitrogen fixation
source: Earth and environmental sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Biological nitrogen (N2) fixation is crucial for incorporating atmospheric N2 into the biosphere. However, its evolutionary trajectory remains enigmatic, particularly given the presumed scarcity of molybdenum (Mo) in Archean seawater prior to oxidative weathering and the apparent early emergence of Mo-based nitrogenase over its vanadium (V)-based alternatives. Here, we integrate partitioning experiments with an extensive analysis of iron-rich sediments through time to investigate the behavior of Mo and V in ancient seawater. Our results suggest that, during the Archean to Paleoproterozoic, dissolved V was removed from seawater more efficiently than Mo, primarily through preferential incorporation into banded iron formations (BIF). Consequently, Mo was likely more available in seawater than commonly assumed, with Archean seawater characterized by higher Mo/V ratios than today. Greater Mo availability relative to V provides a compelling explanation for the earlier evolution of Mo-based nitrogenase despite the absence of widespread oxidative weathering, and helps resolve the apparent paradox surrounding the early evolution of biological N2 fixation.

title: SIP-enabled multi-omics reveals soil microbiome responses to drought and rehydration
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Soil microbial activity, and the balance of anabolic (carbon assimilating) and catabolic (CO2-releasing) processes, control the magnitude and direction of soil carbon fluxes. Soil hydration controls this activity, and with hydroclimate volatility increasing across many regions, microbial responses to drought-rewetting cycles urgently require quantification. We conducted rainfall exclusion experiments at two Mediterranean-type field sites, coupling isotope labeling with multi-omics, to link microbial growth, greenhouse gas fluxes, and the carbon sources driving both. Rehydration shortened apparent cell generation times from years to days within minutes. High-intensity drought lengthened the lag before growth resumed, yet metagenomic inference indicated post-drought enrichment of rapid-growth phenotypes. Drought and rehydration shifted the soil metabolome, implicating specific osmolytes in the microbial response and suggesting metabolite diversity modulates microbial function. These results constrain soil microbial activity rates and mechanisms underlying drought-rewetting responses and motivate further study of carbon cycling under increasingly volatile hydroclimates.

title: Atmospheric O 2 reveals a strengthening ocean carbon sink and a stagnant net land sink since 1990
source: Science
abstract: The global ocean and land biosphere absorb roughly half of fossil fuel carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) emissions. The temporal evolution of these sinks remains difficult to quantify owing to data sparsity. Leveraging 30+ years of atmospheric oxygen (O 2 ) and CO 2 observations, we find that the ocean carbon sink increased by 0.63 ± 0.19 petagrams of carbon per year per decade (Pg C year −1 decade −1 ) (a mean of 2.8 ± 0.4 Pg C year −1 ), accounting for 35% of fossil emissions between 1990 and 2019. The net land sink shows no robust trend (with a mean of 1.0 ± 0.5 Pg C year −1 , accounting for 13% of fossil emissions), despite large decadal variability. These results challenge many process-based model simulations of the land and ocean sinks, questioning their ability to accurately predict future climate states.

title: Depth-Resolved Magnetic Reversal of La0.7Sr0.3Mn1– x Ru x O3-Based Synthetic Antiferromagnets
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Synthetic antiferromagnets based on transition metal oxides provide a versatile platform for engineering magnetic functionalities beyond those of conventional metallic systems. However, the microscopic pathways by which their magnetization reverses remain difficult to determine because conventional magnetic measurements cannot resolve the layer-specific magnetic configurations that emerge during switching. Here, we combine polarized neutron reflectometry, magnetometry, magnetotransport, and an extended Stoner–Wohlfarth model to investigate the magnetization reversal mechanisms in epitaxial La0.7Sr0.3Mn1–xRuxO3/LaNiO3 multilayers. Depth-resolved polarized neutron reflectometry reveals non-collinear magnetic configurations that are hidden from macroscopic probes and identifies the competition between tilted magnetic anisotropy and comparable bilinear and biquadratic interlayer exchange interactions as the origin of the observed behavior. Depending on the magnetic-field orientation, the system undergoes either abrupt switching between magnetic fan and synthetic antiferromagnetic states or a gradual opening of the magnetic fan. Our results establish the intimate connection between magnetic anisotropy, interlayer exchange, and reversal dynamics in oxide synthetic antiferromagnets, revealing correlated oxides as a powerful platform for tuning the balance between competing interactions and engineering tailored magnetic reversal pathways and functionalities.

title: Structural Insights into Proton Exchange Membrane Water Electrolyzers after Long-Term Operation Using Advanced 3D Focused Ion Beam–Scanning Electron Microscopy Tomography
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Proton exchange membrane water electrolyzers (PEMWEs) are key to sustainable hydrogen production, but their long-term performance is limited by degradation, particularly in the membrane electrode assembly (MEA), which remains a barrier to commercial viability. Moreover, the need for corrosion-resistant materials and the intricate fabrication of bipolar plates and porous transport layers (PTLs) further impede large-scale deployment and account for a major share of the stack cost. Because lifetime and replacement costs are strongly influenced by the local microstructure and contact conditions, especially at the anode/PTL interface, a multiscale characterization approach combining 3D focused ion beam–scanning electron microscopy (FIB–SEM) with time-of-flight mass spectrometry is used to investigate degradation in an MEA after several thousand hours of operation under industrially relevant conditions. The 3D reconstruction and ppm-level chemical mapping show that local contact heterogeneities at welds in an expanded-metal mesh PTL act as degradation hotspots. At these sites, intensified catalyst utilization accelerates iridium dissolution, driving iridium migration and deposition as extended filaments into the membrane. Concurrently, membrane voids are formed beneath these sites, accompanied by iron contamination detected at both contact types. In contrast, general contact regions mainly show a thin redeposition layer without voids or filaments. These findings provide a mechanistic framework that links local contact conditions and microstructural heterogeneities to coupled catalyst and membrane degradation, supporting design rules for improved PEMWE durability.

abstract: Mechanocatalysis harnesses ubiquitous mechanical energy for sustainable chemical transformations, but its development is hindered by conceptual fragmentation. This review proposes a process-oriented framework, deconstructing mechanocatalysis into four sequential stages: energy coupling, transduction, charge transport, and electronic behavior. This framework provides a mechanistic basis for the rational design of mechanocatalytic systems, paving the way for standardized evaluation and broader applications.

title: Cu-Doped Highly Porous SnO2 for Long-Lasting Acidic CO2 Electroreduction at 1000 mA cm–2
source: ACS Energy Letters: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) to formic acid (HCOOH) provides a carbon-neutral route. SnO2-based catalysts suffer from limited activity and instability at industrial current densities. We develop a Cu-doped highly porous SnO2 catalyst (SnO2-Cu) that enhances activity and stabilizes the SnO2 framework. The porous structure exposes numerous active sites while confining local OH– within the bulk acid electrolyte, enabling high-current-density operation. Cu doping strengthens CO2 chemisorption and Sn–O bond covalency, boosting CO2RR activity while suppressing SnO2 self-reduction. SnO2-Cu sustains 1000 mA cm–2 for 19 h with 98.5% FE and 800 mA cm–2 for 72 h with 94.1% FE in a flow cell at pH 1.82. It achieves a HCOOH production cost of 722.7 USD tonne–1 in a solid-state electrolyte (SSE) device calculated based on onshore wind power, demonstrating economic competitiveness. This work demonstrates that rational Cu doping of porous SnO2 addresses activity and durability limits, offering an effective platform for high-rate, economically viable HCOOH electrosynthesis.

title: Regulation of Anionic Redox Reaction Voltage by Energy Band Modulation for Li-Rich Cathodes
source: ACS Energy Letters: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Anionic redox reaction (ARR) promises high energy density for Li-rich cathodes yet suffers from severe voltage decay. Here, we investigate ARR voltage modulation in a Li2S-modified quasi-solid Li-rich cathode (Li2S-LRM), which exhibits a distinct low-voltage ARR plateau (2.0–2.8 V). Combining in situ XRD, S K-edge XANES, EELS, Ar-etched XPS and DFT calculations, we validate in situ electrochemical sulfur doping. Upon cycling, the material forms bulk LixS/Li–S–O species alongside a dominant Li2SO3/Li2SO4 polyanion interphase that realizes oxygen trapping. Vacancy-cluster formation facilitates reversible S-involved charge compensation, where sulfur redox activity progressively intensifies during long cycling. Enabled by the band-modulation and oxygen-trapping effects, Li2S-LRM achieves a high average Coulombic efficiency of 99.6% and suppressed voltage decay (0.28 vs. 0.83 mV cycle–1 for pristine LRM). This work deepens mechanistic insights into ARR and provides rational design guidance for high-performance anionic-redox cathodes.

title: Spatiotemporal Molecular Control of Crystallization for Efficient Perovskite/Organic Tandem Photovoltaics
source: ACS Energy Letters: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Perovskite/organic tandem solar cells (PO-TSCs) offer a route toward overcoming the efficiency limitations of single-junction photovoltaics. However, wide-bandgap (WBG) perovskite sub-cells limit their performance, where uncontrolled crystallization leads to compositional heterogeneity, defect accumulation, and severe halide phase segregation. Here, we develop a template-bridge dual-control (TBDC) strategy using 2-thiophenemethylammonium bromide (2-ThMAB). Precisely controlling the introduction timing and spatial distribution of 2-ThMAB maximizes molecular regulation of crystallization. Surface-anchored 2-ThMAB molecules act as growth templates to induce (100) crystal growth, while grain-boundary-localized molecules regulate halide migration through molecular bridging, enabling homogeneous crystallization. The WBG perovskite films exhibit enhanced out-of-plane (100) orientation, reduced defect density, and suppressed halide phase segregation. Consequently, the optimized WBG device achieves a champion power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 20.13% with improved operational stability. Integrated into PO-TSCs, the optimized WBG sub-cells deliver a PCE of 26.62%. This strategy enables concurrent control of crystallization and halide redistribution of efficient, stable tandem photovoltaics.

title: Controllable Synthesis of Porous Core–Shell NiCo Bimetallic Selenides for High-Performance Supercapacitors
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Metal–organic framework (MOF)-derived electrode materials suffer from poor conductivity and structural instability. Herein, a porous core–shell NiCo bimetallic selenide (NiCo PBA–Se) is synthesized via a multistep liquid-phase transformation followed by low-temperature selenization. A Zeolitic Imidazolate Framework-67 (ZIF-67) shell is first epitaxially grown on a Ni-MOF core to construct a core–shell MOF hybrid as the precursor for the preparation of subsequent electrode materials. Unlike conventional methods that convert only the outer MOF layer, the precisely controlled ion-exchange process converts both the inner Ni-MOF and outer ZIF-67 into a NiCo-PBA precursor while preserving the core–shell spherical morphology. Gas-phase selenization at 350 °C yields the target product, which retains a three-dimensional porous spherical architecture composed of stacked ultrathin nanosheets. Ni and Co are uniformly incorporated into the selenide lattice, forming a single-phase (Ni, Co)Se2 solid solution that shortens ion transport paths and increases active sites. Kinetic analysis reveals a synergistic combination of diffusion-controlled and capacitance-controlled charge storage, enabling rapid charge/discharge. In three-electrode tests, NiCo PBA–Se delivers a specific capacitance of 1642 F·g–1 (738.9 C·g–1) at 1 A·g–1. The assembled asymmetric supercapacitor achieves an energy density of 42.52 Wh·kg–1 at 775 W·kg–1 and powers an electronic timer for 20 min. This work demonstrates the effectiveness of the MOF-on-MOF strategy with full conversion of both core and shell and simultaneous maintenance of the core–shell structure for constructing high-performance multimetal selenides.

title: Engineering Ultrathin, Tough Polymer Networks for Stable Lithium Metal Anode Interphases
source: ACS Energy Letters: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Interfacial degradation and dendritic lithium (Li) growth remain critical bottlenecks for practical Li metal batteries (LMBs). Herein, we introduce a tough, ion-conductive poly(2-(dimethylamino)ethyl methacrylate) (pDMAEMA) nanolayer on Li metal via photo-initiated chemical vapor deposition (piCVD). The photo-mediated, solvent-free piCVD enables nanometer-scale coatings with systematic control over photo-crosslinking and chain entanglement without compromising Li surface integrity. This systematic control yields an optimized polymer network balancing toughness (36.3 MJ m–3) and viscoelasticity (10.3% linear viscoelastic strain limit) to accommodate repeated Li volume changes. Furthermore, interactions between pDMAEMA and PF6– anions promote a mechanically durable LiF-rich solid electrolyte interphase, thereby supporting uniform Li deposition. Pouch-type bi-cells employing the optimized 100 nm polymer-coated Li anode achieve an energy density of 338 Wh kg–1 and 80% capacity retention after 90 cycles under practical conditions (N/P = 2, E/C = 3 g Ah–1). This ultrathin, tough polymer network offers a promising design principle for high-energy LMBs.

title: Simultaneous Selective Recognition of Two Different Anions within a Hydrogen/Halogen-Bonding Cage
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The search for selective anion receptors that can function in water is a longstanding challenge in supramolecular chemistry, motivated by anions’ fundamental roles (and potential applications) in biological, environmental, and industrial processes. Here, we incorporate halogen and hydrogen bond donors into an easy-to-prepare organic cage molecule and demonstrate that this can bind anions at either or both of a halogen-bonding pocket and hydrogen-bonding pockets depending on the nature of the anions and the solvent. The halogen-bonding pocket comprising six bromopyridinium donors is a potent host for iodide anions and can selectively bind this guest in water as strongly as biological iodide binders (Ka = 43,000 M–1 measured by 1H NMR spectroscopy) with the exclusion of other halide anions. In DMSO/water mixtures, the hydrogen-bonding pockets are able to recognize chloride anions, resulting in the formation of mixed anion iodide/chloride complexes with an iodide bound in the center of the cage and chlorides in the peripheral binding sites. This demonstrates the exquisite selectivity afforded by halogen-bonding systems and reveals a general route to a range of supramolecular anion hosts that bind multiple guests in different locations.

title: Breaking the “Micro-Size Inversion” Paradox via a Surface-Chemistry-Driven Molecular Sieving Membrane for Ambient Lithium–Air Batteries
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Lithium–air batteries suffer from moisture-induced parasitic reactions and electrolyte evaporation in ambient air. A fundamental challenge is the “micro-size inversion” paradox, where H2O (0.275 nm) is smaller than O2 (0.346 nm), rendering conventional size-based sieving ineffective. Here, we report a composite membrane composed of polydimethylsiloxane and fluorinated vinyl-functionalized covalent organic framework (COF-VF) to break this selectivity barrier. By grafting 1H,1H,2H,2H-perfluorodecyl groups onto a vinyl-functionalized covalent organic framework (COF-V), we establish a surface-chemistry-driven sieving mechanism. This design creates a molecular-level hydrogen-bond-repellent barrier that specifically inhibits polar H2O penetration while maintaining high nonpolar O2 flux, effectively decoupling the permeability-hydrophobicity trade-off. Molecular dynamics simulations corroborate this mechanism, demonstrating that the COF-VF exhibits significantly reduced adsorption affinity toward H2O compared to the pristine COF-V. In 40% RH ambient air, the battery equipped with this membrane delivers a discharge capacity of 3596 mAh g–1 and sustains cycling for 2700 h (270 cycles), a 10.8-fold improvement over unprotected cells. Advanced characterizations via DRT and DEMS confirm that the membrane promotes reversible Li2O2 formation and significantly suppresses LiOH accumulation. This work provides a multiscale strategy for molecular-level selective separation in practical energy storage.

title: Low-Temperature-Mediated Lamellar–Micelle Assembly of Wrinkled Mesoporous Carbon Nanospheres with Aligned Pores and High Interconnectivity
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Mesoporous structures with highly permeable channels are of great significance for fast diffusion; however, the delicate engineering of straightforward pores remains quite limited, with most of mesostructures are tortuous pores derived from spherical micelle assembly. Herein, we explore a novel lamellar–micelle assembly approach that enables to generate a type of wrinkled mesoporous carbon nanospheres with highly interconnected divergent mesopores. In place of the conventional spherical micelles, the key for controlling such unusual assembly is determined by the construction of laminar micelles (copolymer L121/F127 composite) and heterogeneous growth on sedimented F127 seeds at a low temperature of 5 °C. The fabricated wrinkled mesoporous carbon nanospheres after template removal possess a particle size at ∼910 nm, a high surface area of 315 m2 g–1, a uniform pore size at 36 nm, as well as radial mesochannels with high interconnectivity up to 96%. Further regulation on the reaction temperature and template ratio allows for a high tunability over the pore size and wrinkle degree. When employed as a sodium storage anode, the radially aligned large-pore structure drastically facilitates charge transport and electrolyte penetration, thus delivering rate capability (142 mAh g–1 at 10 A g–1) and long-term cyclability (90.5% retention after 1000 cycles at 2 A g–1) compared to commercial hard carbon. Our work underscores a particular assembly pathway through lamellar micelles as an effective approach for building up ultrafast mesopore highways toward promising diffusion-related applications.

title: Specific Amino Acid Imaging of Protein Condensates in Live Cells by Stimulated Raman Scattering Microscopy
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Intracellular protein condensates formed by liquid–liquid phase separation have gained increasing attention in recent years due to their key roles in many physiological and pathological processes. However, fluorescence imaging of protein condensates is limited by the bulky fluorescent tags that could perturb the protein localization and interaction. Imaging techniques that can visualize protein condensates in live cells with minimal perturbations remain lacking. Here, we develop a strategy to image intracellular protein condensates by coupling stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) microscopy to specific amino acid labeling. Different types of amino acids are found to exhibit distinct incorporation patterns in the live cells. By metabolic labeling of deuterated tyrosine-d4 and arginine-d7, ALS-related fused in sarcoma (FUS) protein condensates can be visualized with a high specificity. In addition, two-color pulse-chase imaging reveals protein translation arrest in FUS condensates under stress conditions. Furthermore, heterogeneous tyrosine phosphorylation is imaged in live cells and FUS condensates based on the Raman blue shift of phosphorylated tyrosine-d4. Thus, our technique to image specific amino acids by SRS provides a new platform to visualize the metabolic turnover and post-translational modifications of protein condensates in live cells with minimal perturbation.

title: Visible-Light-Driven Dearomatization via Electrocyclic Ring Expansion for Solar Energy Storage
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Molecular solar thermal (MOST) energy storage compounds capture solar photon energy in the strained chemical bonds of metastable photoisomers and release it on demand as heat, yet simultaneously achieving visible-light absorption and high energy storage density has remained a persistent challenge. Here we introduce 9-aryl acridine N-oxides as MOST compounds based on visible-light-driven dearomative ring expansion. Irradiation at 470 nm, near the solar irradiance maximum at 482 nm, quantitatively converts these compounds to metastable 1,2-oxazepines, which thermally revert to the parent N-oxides and discharge the stored energy. The system achieves energy storage densities of up to 0.54 MJ/kg, comparable to Dewar anthracenes, while absorbing substantially more red-shifted light and offering nearly 3 orders of magnitude longer storage lifetimes of up to 1.4 years in the solid state. The thermal half-lives of the 1,2-oxazepines are tunable through para-substitution on the aryl ring and solvation, enabling up to a 1,300-fold reduction in half-life. Crucially, the 9-aryl substituent biases the transient oxaziridine intermediate toward selective reversion to the N-oxide over competing decomposition pathways, overcoming the limitations of other acridine N-oxides reported to date. This work establishes light-induced ring expansion as an effective strategy for MOST and expands the scope of viable MOST compounds.

title: Photomediated Chromium-Catalyzed Regio-, Diastereo-, and Enantioselective Deoxygenative Coupling of Activated Allylic and Propargylic Alcohols with Aldehydes
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Chromium-catalyzed asymmetric Nozaki–Hiyama–Kishi (NHK) reaction is a powerful tool for constructing synthetically valuable enantioenriched homoallylic alcohols and allenols. However, catalytic asymmetric NHK-type coupling of allylic or propargylic C–O electrophiles remains largely underdeveloped. Herein, we report a photomediated chromium-catalyzed deoxygenative coupling of activated allylic and propargylic alcohols with aldehydes, enabling the synthesis of a variety of chiral homoallylic alcohols with wide structural diversity and allenols. The reactions were performed under mild conditions, and a wide range of synthetically useful functional groups was found to be well tolerated. Importantly, this method provides a straightforward way for the construction of homoallylic alcohols bearing a chiral quaternary carbon center with high ee and dr. Furthermore, stereodivergent access to all four homoallylic alcohol stereoisomers is realized through orthogonal combinations of Z/E-configured allylic alcohols and R/S-configured ligands. Combined experimental and computational mechanistic studies provided insight into the key catalytic intermediate and the origin of stereocontrol.

title: Hybrid Weakly Coordinated Solvents for Fast-Charging and Wide-Temperature Sodium-Ion Full Batteries
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The application of sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) in wide-temperature and fast-charging scenarios is severely constrained by the performance limitations of electrolytes. Conventional ester-based electrolytes struggle to simultaneously achieve high ionic conductivity, low desolvation energy, and excellent interfacial stability. Herein, we propose a hybrid solvent system comprising ethyl propionate and ethoxy(pentafluoro)cyclotriphosphazene (PFPN), aiming to synergistically enhance the rate capability and temperature adaptability of SIBs. The relatively weak coordination ability of both solvents effectively promotes anion participation in solvation structure, significantly lowering the Na+ desolvation energy barrier and inducing the formation of stable, inorganic-rich electrode/electrolyte interphases. Meanwhile, the dual-solvent combination increases the diversity of solvation configurations and reduces ion clustering, thereby enhancing ionic conductivity. The intrinsic nonflammability and excellent film-forming ability of PFPN further enhance safety and synergistically strengthen interfacial stability. Therefore, Prussian blue||hard carbon full cells operate stably over a wide temperature range from −50 to 100 °C. Notably, ampere-hour-level pouch cells deliver a capacity retention of 86.3% after 300 cycles at 25 °C and maintain stable operation for over 100 cycles even at −20 and 80 °C. This solvent synergy strategy offers a practical new pathway for the development of electrolytes for SIBs in extreme environments.

title: Functional Specialization of Coordination Spheres Enables Site-Selective Aromatic C–H Isotope Exchange in Ni Single-Atom Catalysts
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Engineering single-atom catalysts has predominantly focused on tailoring the primary coordination sphere, whereas whether distinct coordination spheres can be endowed with independent catalytic functions remains largely unexplored. Here, we demonstrate the functional specialization of coordination spheres by constructing a phosphorus-modified Ni–N2O2 single-atom catalyst for site-selective C–H deuteration. Advanced spectroscopic characterizations and theoretical calculations show that phosphorus is incorporated outside the preserved primary Ni–N2O2 coordination environment and support an O-linked phosphorus environment as a preferential second-sphere motif. This architecture decouples substrate recognition from catalytic activation. Specifically, second-sphere phosphorus selectively recognizes and anchors the amino group of haloanilines to dictate deuteration site selectivity, whereas the preserved primary Ni–N2O2 coordination sphere promotes H2 activation and undergoes H2-assisted regeneration following D2O-induced hydroxylation, facilitated by P–O–Ni electronic communication, thereby sustaining efficient catalytic turnover. Consequently, the catalyst achieves highly site-selective C–H deuteration of chloro-, bromo-, and iodoanilines using H2 and D2O while completely preserving carbon–halogen bonds, whereas the phosphorus-free analogue exhibits negligible activity. This work identifies the structural origin and catalytic function of second-sphere phosphorus and establishes functional specialization of coordination spheres as a general design principle for independently programming substrate recognition and catalytic turnover in single-atom catalysis.

title: Magnetic Resonance Silent Activatable Probe with Massive Signal Amplification for Rapid Detection of Inflammation-Associated Fibrogenesis
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Biomarker-specific molecular imaging is vital in precision medicine. However, a fundamental challenge of most molecular imaging methods is the difficulty of distinguishing specific molecular signal from nonspecific signal arising from the distribution of the molecular probe. This is even more pronounced in metabolically active organs such as the kidney and liver where the probe may concentrate prior to elimination. As a result, almost all molecular imaging relies on delayed imaging to achieve specificity, but this constrains clinical throughput and impedes rapid assessment of the diseased organ. Here, we report a magnetic resonance (MR) probe, Fe(II)-IAFP2, which combines 3 drivers of relaxivity enhancement to decouple disease specificity from probe distribution. Fe(II)-IAFP2 is MR-silent in its Fe(II) state, producing negligible MR signal even at high concentrations. In inflammatory, fibrogenic microenvironments common to many diseases, rapid oxidation to Fe(III) activates MR enhancement, while reversible aldehyde-mediated binding to remodeled extracellular matrix further amplifies relaxivity and promotes retention at the site of tissue injury. This dual activation–retention mechanism enables robust signal generation within minutes of administration. In mouse models of renal and liver fibrogenesis, Fe(II)-IAFP2 generated disease-associated MR contrast within minutes after intravenous administration. Together, this work demonstrates an effective strategy for rapid, activity-based molecular MR imaging through the combination of pathological activation and complementary tissue retention.

title: Ammonia-Driven Nanoscale Surface Restructuring of Copper Catalysts during Nitrate Reduction Reaction
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The electrolyte and applied potential are known to impact a catalyst’s structure and performance, yet the role of reaction intermediates and products in driving surface evolution remains largely unexplored. Here, using electrochemical atomic force microscopy, we show that the dynamic restructuring of copper (Cu) surfaces during nitrate reduction reaction (NO3RR) directly correlates with the rate and selectivity of ammonia (NH3) formation. At moderate overpotentials, where nitrite formation dominates, lateral expansion of Cu terraces is observed, whereas rapid NH3 formation at higher cathodic potentials induces Cu adislands enriched in low-coordinated step sites, revealing distinct restructuring pathways that accompany the transition from nitrite- to ammonia-selective NO3RR. These transformations are rationalized by an NH3-mediated Cu dissolution-redeposition mechanism. Our results identify reaction products as active modulators of catalyst surface structure, establishing a framework for understanding reaction-driven catalyst restructuring and enabling in situ control of catalyst surfaces through the interfacial reaction environment.

title: Acetaldehyde-Mediated Direct Conversion of Air to Nitric Acid
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The sustainable synthesis of nitric acid (HNO3) directly from air via N2 oxidation is a dream reaction but remains a long-standing challenge, owing to formidable thermodynamic and kinetic barriers. Here, we report a photoassisted thermocatalytic strategy in which acetaldehyde as a key medium enables efficient N2 oxidation to HNO3 under mild conditions. Acetaldehyde is oxidized to peracetic acid over 316L stainless steel, which subsequently generates radicals (CH3COOO•) under visible-light irradiation. These CH3COOO• radicals are highly reactive and can oxidize N2 at 200 °C and near-ambient pressures (1–5 bar), affording an HNO3 formation rate of 110.8 μmol h–1 with a concentration of 13,961 ppm and an N2 conversion of 0.45% within 2 h─approximately 2 to 4 orders of magnitude higher than previously reported systems. Notably, the kinetic irrelevance of H2O enables operation in a gas-phase flow configuration, allowing continuous and stable HNO3 production and gram-scale accumulation at the laboratory scale. This work introduces a groundbreaking reaction paradigm that couples organic radical chemistry and surface catalysis, offering a scalable and energy-efficient pathway for the green synthesis of HNO3.

title: Control of Charge Carrier Dynamics and Bandgap Renormalization in CdS Quantum Dot Hybrids by Interface Polarity
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Charge carrier dynamics in wurtzite CdS quantum dots (QDs) form the basis for applications in optoelectronics and photocatalysis. We demonstrate that the quantum dynamics, energy gaps, and energy level alignments at CdS QD interfaces can be controlled by the polarity of the CdS QD surface. By performing nonadiabatic molecular dynamics simulations within a density-functional tight-binding framework, we demonstrate a strong dependence of photoinitiated processes in CdS QDs/graphene nanoribbon (GNR) hybrids on interface polarity. At room temperature, hole transfer is accelerated by a factor of 2 and exciton lifetime is enhanced by nearly an order of magnitude when the CdS QD surface is switched from polar to nonpolar. Remarkably, the interfacial bandgap for the polar QD/GNR hybrid is reduced to half upon heating from 0 K to room temperature, while it remains nearly unchanged for the nonpolar hybrid. At an intermediate temperature, the ultrafast charge separation is maintained; however, charge recombination shows the opposite trend relative to room temperature. The polar interface exhibits a longer lifetime than the nonpolar interface, due to weakened electron–phonon Fröhlich interaction and decreased gap renormalization. The strong and highly nonlinear dependence of bandgap renormalization and carrier dynamics on temperature in the polar QD/GNR hybrid is associated with significant structural reconstruction, which is absent in the nonpolar counterpart. The demonstrated control of excited-state processes by interface polarity and the strong dependence of the dynamics and energy level alignment on temperature provide key fundamental insights for informed design of modern materials for optoelectronics and energy conversion.
