title: A Molybdoenzyme Mediates Carbon–Sulfur Bond Making and Breaking in Ergothioneine Biosynthesis
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The molybdopterin-dependent ergothioneine synthase (MES) from Caldithrix abyssi is the first molybdoenzyme known to catalyze the formation of carbon–sulfur bonds. To complete its catalytic cycle, this bifunctional enzyme desulfurates l-cysteine at a pyridoxal 5′-phosphate binding site and transfers the harvested sulfur atom (S0) to the molybdenum center of a bis-molybdopterin guanine dinucleotide cofactor more than 50 Å away. Subsequently, the sulfurated Mo-center transfers the labile sulfur atom onto the imidazole ring of Nα-trimethyl histidine (TMH). Combining experimental observations from cryo-electron microscopy, X-ray crystallography, X-ray absorption spectroscopy, sequence-activity correlation, and substrate-specificity studies, we delineate the structural basis for long-distance sulfur transfer via a persulfide relay, the identity of the imidazole sulfurating species, and key sequence motifs that are indispensable for activity. Furthermore, the reversibility of MES-mediated sulfurization of TMH under physiological conditions suggests that ergothioneine may serve as a soluble reservoir of oxidizing equivalents, supporting anaerobic metabolism in deep-branching bacteria such as C. abyssi.

title: Empowering HFIP as a Radical Trifluoromethylating Reagent by Photoelectrochemical Iron Catalysis
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The development of practical synthetic methods for incorporating trifluoromethyl (CF3) groups into organic scaffolds is of paramount importance in medicinal chemistry, as such modifications profoundly modulate the physicochemical properties of drug candidates. 1,1,1,3,3,3-Hexafluoro-2-propanol (HFIP) is widely utilized as a unique solvent in synthetic chemistry and also represents a promising CF3 source due to its high availability and low cost. Here we report an unprecedented photoelectrochemical iron-catalyzed protocol for radical trifluoromethylation that employs commercially accessible HFIP as the CF3 radical precursor. This method enables efficient trifluoromethylation of unactivated arenes, heteroarenes, and alkenes with a broad substrate scope and excellent functional group tolerance. Notably, this photoelectrocatalytic system is readily scalable for practical synthetic applications, and its utility has been demonstrated in the trifluoromethylation of peptides, allowing preferential modification of tryptophan residues in a chemoselective fashion.

title: Non-ionic Phthalocyanine Additives Enable Synergistic Passivation and Strain Buffering in Stable Perovskite Solar Cells
source: ACS Energy Letters: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The long-term stability of high-efficiency n-i-p perovskite solar cells is limited by coupled defect migration, residual lattice strain, and thermal–mechanical degradation. Here, we develop a non-ionic, interface-enriched zinc phthalocyanine derivative, 4PCSZnPc, as a molecular stabilizer for simultaneous defect anchoring and strain buffering. Unlike ionic additives that may introduce mobile species, 4PCSZnPc is distributed throughout the film, with enrichment near the buried SnO2/perovskite interface. Peripheral N/O/S heteroatoms coordinate with under-coordinated Pb2+ sites, while the Zn-regulated macrocyclic center interacts with iodide-related defects, forming dual-site Lewis acid–base anchoring. Meanwhile, the rigid phthalocyanine framework reduces residual tensile stress and may hinder strain-assisted ion migration. These combined effects of defect passivation and strain buffering reduce non-radiative recombination, improve film uniformity, and enhance thermal robustness. Consequently, 4PCSZnPc-treated devices achieve a champion power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 26.88% (certified 26.74%), a T80 lifetime of 1358 h under 1-sun at 85 °C, and 95% retention after 200 thermal cycles, providing a design principle for future thermally resilient photovoltaics.

title: A Double-Tethered Metallacyclobutadiene Catalyst for Cyclic Polymer Synthesis
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The synthesis, characterization, and catalytic polymerization results of an unprecedented double-tethered metallacyclobutadiene complex (4) are discussed. Complex 4 is active for the polymerization of acetylenes. Complex 4 polymerizes tert-butylacetylene to form cyclic poly(tert-butylacetylene). Evidence for a cyclic polymer topology comes from size exclusion chromatography (SEC) and intrinsic viscosity (η) measurements. This unusual reactivity of complex 4 toward a tert-alkylacetylene is attributed to its fluxional behavior, which arises from the double tethering of an yne-ol proligand (2) that facilitates monomer access and catalytic turnover. The preliminary scope of this complex design is demonstrated through modification of the yne-ol proligand, which afforded two additional double-tethered metallacyclobutadiene complexes 10 and 11 that are also catalytically active for polymerization.

title: Electric-Field-Driven Surface Ionic Transport on Hydroxylated SiO2 Governs Transient Leakage and Hybrid Bonding Reliability
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Cu/SiO2 hybrid bonding is critical for 3D integrated circuit packaging, where dielectric surface activation impacts bonding quality and long-term reliability. NaOH-based wet chemical activation is a promising approach for a scalable and cost-effective processing under ambient conditions. However, this route introduces residual ions at the SiO2 surface, raising concerns regarding electrical leakage and dielectric stability. In this study, electric-field-driven surface ionic transport on NaOH-activated SiO2 and its role in transient leakage and hybrid bonding reliability were investigated. Reversible and polarity-dependent transient current peaks observed in cyclic electrical measurements provide evidence for electric-field-driven migration of the mobile ionic species at the SiO2 interface. In addition, higher NaOH concentrations promoted greater residual Na+ accumulation and intensified transient leakage peaks, supporting the selection of 0.5 M NaOH as an effective activation condition. Systematic decoupling experiments demonstrate that residual mobile Na+ ions are the dominant contributors to the transient leakage current rather than fixed hydroxyl groups. Quantitative analysis reveals Na+ surface mobility of approximately 3 × 10–10 m2V–1s–1, an order-of-magnitude upper-bound estimate that is consistent between constant-bias and ramped-bias measurements and about six orders of magnitude higher than that in bulk SiO2, suggesting a surface-dominated transport. An optimized 3 min deionized water (DI) rinse reduces the mobile Na+ population below the electrical detection limit and decreases the Na 1s XPS intensity by roughly an order of magnitude, suppressing the transient leakage to near-baseline levels while maintaining hydrophilicity and achieving the SiO2–SiO2 bonding strength of 19.7 ± 1.8 MPa, comparable to Ar plasma activation. The leakage measurements were performed on Cu/SiO2 damascene comb structures, whereas the bonding validation addresses the dielectric part of the hybrid-bonding interface; Cu–Cu contact and long-term stress testing remain to be verified. This work provides a framework for understanding electric-field-driven surface ionic transport and practical guidelines for contamination control of the dielectric surface in wet-activated Cu/SiO2 hybrid bonding.

title: A Rutin–Glycyrrhizic Acid Self-Assembled Nanohydrogel Promotes Early Osteogenic Differentiation Potential and Antioxidant Activity via Synergistic Inhibition of the IL-1β/NF-κB Axis
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Plant-derived natural compounds have gained increasing attention in biomaterial development due to their intrinsic bioactivity and favorable biocompatibility. The anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and osteogenic properties of rutin and glycyrrhizic acid have rendered them increasingly attractive candidates for therapeutic biomaterial development. However, their poor bioavailability significantly restricts their broad biomedical applications. Inspired by a supramolecular self-assembly strategy, we successfully constructed a rutin–glycyrrhizic acid nanohydrogel (RU–GA). The microstructure and formation mechanism were investigated through experimental characterization and computational simulations. Rutin (RU) and glycyrrhizic acid (GA) self-assemble into a carrier-free hydrogel in aqueous solution via hydrogen bonding and π–π stacking interactions, exhibiting favorable injectability, shapeability, and stability. RU–GA can disperse in water and release rutin–glycyrrhizic acid nanoparticles (RG NPs) with homogeneous particle sizes, while the hydrogel material possesses degradation and sustained-release properties. The bioavailability of RU and GA is synergistically improved through size effects and continuous release. Notably, the RU–GA hydrogel significantly promotes antioxidant activity and early osteogenic differentiation potential relative to the individual monomer components. Bioinformatics analysis further suggested that these bioactivities are associated with IL1B. Il1b knockdown experiments validated that RU and GA may synergistically suppress IL-1β-mediated NF-κB activation, thereby reducing oxidative stress and enhancing early osteogenic differentiation potential. Collectively, the rutin–glycyrrhizic acid nanohydrogel (RU–GA) represents a promising functional biomaterial, providing a strategy for the broad application of natural compounds in biomedical and related fields.

title: Enzyme-Powered Nanomotor as a Mobile Immobilization Carrier for Facilitating the Enzymatic Degradation of Chitin
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Chitin, the second most abundant biomass after cellulose on earth, can be degraded into chitin oligosaccharides (CHOS), which hold considerable commercial value. However, the sustainable bioconversion of chitin is impeded by its mass transfer limitations and poor accessibility of chitinase to the substrate. Herein, a Janus urease-powered nanomotor (JUNM) was synthesized via a facile approach and employed as an immobilization carrier for chitinase (Chi B) to improve the enzymatic production of CHOS. It was demonstrated that the structural asymmetry of JUNM enabled the asymmetric decomposition of urea, thereby achieving more efficient self-propulsion at low urea concentrations than a symmetric urease-powered nanomotor (UNM). The self-propulsive behavior of the resulting immobilized chitinase nanomotor (Chi B@JUNM) enhanced its enzymatic performance. Compared with the passive counterpart, the enhanced enzyme–substrate contact induced by the autonomous movement and by the substrate adsorption resulting from electrostatic interactions improved the substrate affinity (a 50% decrease in apparent Km) and led to a 53% increase in catalytic efficiency (apparent kcat·Km–1). Moreover, the immobilization of Chi B on JUNM exhibited typical advantages of enhanced stability and reusability. As a result, the final CHOS yield achieved by the self-propelled Chi B@JUNM (with 50 mM urea) was 1.34 and 2.15 times the yield of passive Chi B@JUNM and free Chi B, respectively. Taken together, the reported enzyme-powered nanomotor provided an efficient platform for chitin degradation and paved the way for the design of advanced immobilization carriers to facilitate enzymatic reactions.

title: A Multicyclic Catalytic Network Enabling ROS Amplification, Metabolic Disruption, and Immune Modulation for Antitumor–Antibacterial Therapy
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Intratumoral bacteria are increasingly recognized as important regulators of tumor progression, immune suppression, and metastasis, whereas current therapeutic strategies remain insufficient to address the coupled tumor–bacteria microenvironment. Here, we report a multicyclic catalytic network (VBC-Net) that integrates alkaline polyoxovanadate with a Bi2WO6–CuSx p–n heterojunction for coordinated antitumor–antibacterial immunotherapy. Unlike conventional single-mechanism nanozymes, VBC-Net establishes interconnected catalytic cycles that sustain ROS amplification, oxygen activation, and glutathione depletion, thereby converting transient catalytic activity into persistent oxidative stress. Simultaneously, the alkaline microenvironment and Bi-associated interference with respiratory-chain-related processes may contribute to metabolic perturbation, coupling oxidative stress with metabolic disruption. VBC-Net is further associated with dendritic-cell maturation, enhanced T-cell infiltration, and pro-inflammatory immune modulation, suggesting remodeling of the tumor–bacteria–immune microenvironment. In murine 4T1 tumor and MRSA-infected models, VBC-Net achieves pronounced tumor suppression, bacterial clearance, reduced metastatic progression, and accelerated wound healing with good biocompatibility. This work establishes a multicyclic catalytic strategy for targeting complex tumor-associated ecosystems and provides a promising framework for antitumor–antibacterial therapy.

title: Molecular Anchoring and Multiscale Porosity Synergize in 3D Printed Polyimide Composites for High-Temperature Thermal Management
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The large-scale application of energy storage systems such as lithium-ion batteries, which feature high energy density and considerable flammability risks, has created an urgent demand for thermal management materials that offer lightweight construction, high-temperature resistance, efficient insulation, and customizable shaping. Polyimide (PI) is a promising candidate; however, its additive manufacturing is constrained by the high temperatures required for thermal imidization and the severe shrinkage that accompanies this process. To overcome these limitations, herein, an interfacial chemical anchoring strategy is introduced, through which amino-functionalized hollow glass microspheres (HGMs) are covalently integrated into a soluble PI matrix. The achieved composite ink is well-suited for vapor-induced phase separation (VIPS)-assisted direct ink writing (DIW), allowing in situ porosification. The 3D printed constructs thus feature a hierarchical thermal resistance architecture, including macroscopic air gaps from printing, microporous networks derived from phase separation, and hollow HGM cavities, which synergistically suppresses solid conduction, gas convection, and thermal radiation. In addition, the covalently anchored microspheres also serve as crosslinking nodes, enhancing compressive strength. The optimized composites achieve a 35% reduction in density, shrinkage below 5%, a thermal conductivity of 0.048 W·m–1·K–1, and a nearly fourfold improvement in compressive strength. Together, these results demonstrate that the synergy between interfacial chemical anchoring and VIPS-assisted DIW provides a versatile platform for engineering lightweight, high-strength insulation components with tailored geometries for demanding high-temperature applications.

title: Superhydrophobic Self-Cleaning Polyvinyl Alcohol-Based Films for Enhanced Passive Radiative Cooling and Durability
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Developing sustainable and durable superhydrophobic passive radiative cooling materials is crucial for reducing building energy consumption in a warming world, yet conventional radiative cooling materials often rely on nonrenewable polymeric substrates and fluorosiloxane-based surface modifiers, and present materials have poor durability of superhydrophobicity under harsh conditions, limiting their environmental sustainability and long-term applicability. Herein, we develop a biomass-derived superhydrophobic radiative cooling film by integrating waste straw cellulose with starch and poly(vinyl alcohol) as a renewable film-forming matrix, TiO2 as a solar-reflection filler, and a fluorosiloxane-free surface engineering strategy. The resulting cooling film exhibits a solar reflectance of 76.06% and an infrared emissivity of 96.66% within the atmospheric window. The film achieves an average temperature reduction of 28.2 °C relative to the blank cavity during the test period. Moreover, the superhydrophobic surface imparts excellent self-cleaning capability and enables the film to withstand acid/alkali corrosion, water washing, and prolonged high-temperature treatment (>100 °C for 8 h), demonstrating its robust environmental durability. Beyond passive thermal regulation, the cooling film exhibits an excellent water collection rate of 2476.2 mg cm–2 h–1. The combination of renewable agricultural waste as the structural feedstock, fluorosiloxane-free superhydrophobicity, efficient solar reflection, high infrared emission, and multifunctional environmental stability distinguishes the cooling film from conventional petroleum-based radiative cooling systems. This work provides a sustainable materials-design strategy for converting agricultural waste into multifunctional radiative cooling materials with potential applications in energy-efficient building envelopes and sustainable thermal management.

title: Effective Suppression of Cu+-Migration Assisted Degradation in Perovskite Solar Cells with Cu2O as the Hole Transport Layer
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Formamidinium-based double-cation perovskite solar cells exhibit rapid performance degradation when the Cu2O hole transport layer is in direct contact with the perovskite. This degradation is attributed to Cu+ migration into the perovskite lattice, causing structural distortion and the formation of CuI and PbI2. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy detects Cu+ ions even at the antipodal surface of the perovskite, indicating long-range diffusion of the Cu+ ions, probably through grain-boundary migration. To suppress this, a thin film of benzotriazole is introduced at the Cu2O/perovskite interface as a diffusion-blocking layer that also provides mild surface passivation. Adding poly(acrylonitrile-co-methyl acrylate) to the perovskite synthesis solution passivates the grain boundaries and further prevents the migration of Cu+ towards the perovskite. These modifications effectively curb Cu+ migration and its reaction with the perovskite. Consequently, p-i-n perovskite solar cells with the architecture ITO/Cu2O/perovskite/C60/BCP/Ag, incorporating both modifications, exhibit a significant improvement in power conversion efficiency, from ≈4.7 to 14.4%.

title: Pneumatic Rigid-Soft Coupled Finger with Self-Powered Triboelectric Tactile Sensing toward Potential Application in Lunar Exploration
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Robotic manipulation in future lunar-surface operations and planetary sample-return missions requires end effectors capable of accommodating irregular objects while maintaining reliable tactile feedback under uncertain contact conditions. Motivated by these challenges, we present a terrestrial proof-of-concept of a pneumatic rigid–soft coupled robotic finger integrating structural regulation and self-powered triboelectric tactile sensing. The finger combines rigid skeletons, fiber-constrained pneumatic chambers, and a finger-pad sensing unit to enable compliant deformation, posture regulation, and tactile perception. A flexible single-electrode triboelectric sensor based on a PDMS-MXene composite generates electrical signals through contact electrification and electrostatic induction without external electrical excitation, while pneumatic actuation, signal acquisition, and computational processing require external power. At an input pressure of 140 kPa, the proximal interphalangeal, distal interphalangeal, and metacarpophalangeal regions achieved bending angles of approximately 84°, 76°, and 65°, respectively. The sensor exhibited stable outputs at contact frequencies of 1–10 Hz and a sensitivity of 0.11 V/kPa over 10–120 kPa. Incorporating 6 wt% MXene increased the output voltage by 50.8% compared with pure PDMS. Combined with a convolutional neural network-long short-term memory model, the system achieved classification accuracies of 97.6% for 10 representative laboratory materials and 99.5% for four surface-roughness levels under controlled terrestrial conditions. Grasping experiments further demonstrated compliant manipulation and tactile perception. These results establish the feasibility of the proposed sensing approach under laboratory conditions, while its applicability to planetary geological materials and space environments remains to be validated.

title: Multiscale Intercalation Strategies for Reconstructing Lamellar MXene Membranes
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Lamellar MXene membranes, constructed by stacking MXene nanosheets to form two-dimensional nanochannels with ultrafast transport and sieving ability, have emerged as a promising platform for molecular and ionic separations as well as osmotic energy harvesting. However, the performance of these MXene membranes is often constrained by swelling-induced unstable nanochannels and monotonous chemistry environments within nanochannels. One of the most effective routes to these challenges lies in the incorporation of functional intercalation matters into the confined nanochannels of MXene, which not only orchestrate interlayer spacing and nanochannel chemistry but also improve stability by forming multiple interactions with neighboring nanosheets. Over the past decade, a series of multiscale intercalation matters have been designed and explored, mainly spanning from ions to small molecules, polymers, and nanomaterials. Despite significant achievements, a timely and comprehensive review that systematically elucidates how various multiscale intercalation matters reconstruct MXene membranes is missing. In this review, we discuss recent advances in intercalation strategies for lamellar MXene membranes, categorized by the chemical nature and dimensionality of the intercalating matters. We underscore their critical roles in modulating both the structural and chemical features of nanochannels, and we systematically analyze the corresponding effects on transport behavior and separation performance. Finally, some key unresolved challenges and future directions are highlighted to guide the design and synthesis of high-performance lamellar MXene membranes.

title: Monolithic Fabrication of Flexible Optoelectronic Neuromorphic Synapses with Bandgap-Engineered Centimeter-Scale SnSe2 van der Waals Layers
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The transition of bandgap energies in two-dimensional (2D) materials driven by their miniaturization opens up opportunities for emerging device technologies unattainable with conventional approaches. Herein, “all” 2D optoelectronic synapse devices are reported employing the transition characteristics of wafer-scale 2D tin diselenide (SnSe2) layers directly grown on polymeric substrates at a low temperature of 300 °C. Specifically, a significant thickness-dependent reduction in their band energy from 0.8 to 0.25 eV enables a “monolithic” fabrication of flexible device arrays composed of extremely thin active/passive components; i.e., n-type semiconducting 2D channels seamlessly interfaced with heavily doped metallic-like 2D electrodes. These 2D/2D interfaces exhibit reliable Ohmic transports without the need for work function engineering of contact metals as well as well-preserved mechanical deformability. A variety of optoelectronic synaptic properties are demonstrated in the all-2D devices, including deformation-invariant plasticity updates, which are implementable for high-accuracy pattern recognition of artificial neural networks (ANNs). This study suggests new methodologies for integrating the dimensionally tunable electrical properties of near atom-thickness materials into their scalable manufacturability for emergent neuromorphic applications.

title: Template Mineralized, Decellularized Matrix-Alginate-Based Bioink Provides Structural Reinforcement in Caprine Ex Vivo Bone Defect Model
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Clinical management of critical-sized bone defects (CSDs) remains a significant surgical problem. Current bioinks fail to support initial loading on bone tissue. In this study, goat-derived decellularized matrix (DCM) was used as a template for controlled mineralization, while alginate improved the printability and cellular viability. DCM proteins acted as a natural template for hydroxyapatite (HA) crystal nucleation and growth, mimicking bone nanocomposite chemistry while enhancing structural reinforcement. HA formation on DCM template was visualized by atomic force microscopy (AFM) analysis, characteristic phosphate (PO43–) peaks in attenuated total reflectance-Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (ATR-FTIR), and the HA-specific (211) diffraction peak in X-ray diffraction (XRD). Mineralized DCM was blended with alginate to formulate printable bioinks. Rheological analysis showed dominant elastic behavior (G′ > G″), shear-thinning flow, and rapid post-shear recovery. Mechanical testing further demonstrated enhanced compressive strength in HA-DCM-alginate constructs. Bioprinting with osteoblast cells demonstrated higher cellular viability in the mineralized ink while enhancing osteogenic differentiation, via both biochemical and biophysical signaling from the mineralized-DCM ink. In an ex vivo defect model, the HA-DCM-alginate system significantly increased the compressive properties of the defect construct, providing immediate structural reinforcement at the defect site. Overall, the current mineralized bioink can provide both mechanical support and bone regeneration and holds promising potential for surgical application.

title: Nanofibrous Thermo-Optical Materials for Spacecraft Passive Thermal Control
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Passive thermal control is essential for spacecraft operating in extreme extraterrestrial environments, where minimizing solar heat absorption while maximizing thermal radiation is critical for maintaining acceptable onboard temperatures without additional energy consumption. title: All 3D-Printed Conducting Polymer Hydrogel-Based Soft Surface Electromyography Electrode Array for Noninvasive Fatigue Assessment
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract High-density surface electromyography (sEMG) electrode arrays allow the recording of rich myoelectric signals and provide a useful approach for monitoring exercise-induced muscle fatigue. However, existing sEMG electrode arrays often suffer from mechanical mismatches between conventional rigid electrodes and soft tissues, as well as complex fabrication processes and limited programmability, which severely constrain the rational design and practical application of sEMG electrode arrays. Herein, we successfully fabricate an eight-channel PEDOT:PSS-PVA hydrogel-based soft sEMG electrode array via a multi-material 3D printing. Through systematic rheological characterization of the composite inks and rational design of a printable three-layer electrode architecture, we achieve seamless interfacial integration and integrated sequential fabrication. The as-prepared sEMG electrode array exhibits exceptional softness comparable to that of human soft tissues (Young’s modulus ∼ 10 kPa), low electrochemical impedance (∼22 Ω), and good electrochemical stability. Leveraging these advantageous properties, our sEMG electrode array enables noninvasive sEMG signal recording and monitoring of fatigue-associated sEMG changes with a high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR > 20 dB) under various grip forces before and after exercise, and captures sEMG changes associated with fatigue progression during repetitive movements. These results validate the capability of our electrode array for high-quality sEMG monitoring of fatigue-associated electrophysiological features and open up promising avenues for future applications such as scientific athletic training.

title: Crystallinity-Dependent Donor Activation in RF-Sputtered SnO2 Electron-Transport Layers and the Interface-Character Origin of Their Predicted Device-Level Consequences
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract SnO2 is the electron-transport layer (ETL) in record n–i–p perovskite solar cells, grown by chemical bath deposition (CBD) without high-temperature crystallization; whether its crystallinity matters remains unresolved. Here, the same RF-sputtering process on fluorine-doped tin oxide (FTO), at room temperature or 300 °C, yields a predominantly amorphous or an FTO-templated polycrystalline rutile film. The measured film and interface properties anchor a calibrated TCAD model and a thirteen-parameter Sobol global sensitivity analysis (>33,000 simulations), which, unlike one-factor-at-a-time sweeps, resolves the interactions among parameters explicitly. At the film level, crystallinity governs donor activation: UPS, XPS, and STEM-EDS show that the amorphous film holds more fluorine yet has a Fermi level farther below the conduction band, so shallow donors attributed to substitutional fluorine exist in both films but are active only in the crystalline one. At the device level, however, the predicted gain arises from the crystalline film's interface rather than its doping. The Ag/SnO2 contact is rectifying on the amorphous film and ohmic on the crystalline one, through interface-state de-pinning rather than a band-offset shift. The Sobol analysis ranks the SnO2/perovskite interface trap density first (total-effect index ≈ 0.66). A degenerately doped film could screen such traps, but the amorphous film's rectification rules out that route; its deficit is interfacial. At its trap density (∼1013 cm–2), only deep acceptor-like states pin the Fermi level (acceptor-fraction index ≈ 0.83). The predicted crystallization gain is +5.6 pp (20.5 → 26.1%). FAPbI3 half-stack PL/TRPL supports this (1.35× longer lifetime on the crystalline ETL) and bounds that interface's trap density to ≲1012 cm–2. Crystalline growth is one route to the de-pinned interface that CBD ETLs reach chemically, provided that interface is preserved. The absolute efficiencies are calibrated predictions; the benefit's sign and the lever ranking are robust.

title: General Synthesis of Functionalized 1,3-Diamines from Azoarenes and Enoates via Electrochemical Annulation and N–N Bond Cleavage Followed by Chemical Reduction
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Despite the widespread utility of N-substituted 1,3-diamines across numerous fields, their selective synthesis directly from readily available feedstocks remains a long-standing challenge. In this context, we report a room-temperature electrochemical protocol for the synthesis of both symmetrical and unsymmetrical N,N′-disubstituted 1,3-diamines through electrochemical transformation of azoarenes with enoates, followed by convergent reduction of the resulting β-amino amides. This method features broad substrate scope, operational simplicity, no need for noble transition-metal catalysts, and high chemoselectivity. Mechanistic studies indicate that the reaction is initiated by the reduction of azoarenes, facilitated by HCOOH, while Zn2+ ions leached from anodic oxidation serve as a Lewis acid to promote intramolecular cyclization via ester amidation. Subsequent cathodic reduction drives N–N bond cleavage to afford the β-amino amide intermediates, thereby endowing azoarenes with dual-nitrogen synthon capability. This work provides a practical platform for the general synthesis of N,N′-difunctionalized 1,3-diamines and convenient late-stage structural editing of biomedicals.

title: Geometry-Driven Ultrahigh Current Density Field Emission from Vertically Oriented MXene Film Edge Emitters
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract MXenes are promising cold cathode materials owing to their high electrical conductivity, solution processability, and tunable surface terminations; however, realizing high-current-density field emission from MXene film emitters remains challenging because their planar two-dimensional geometry generally provides limited field concentration and restricts the number of field-activated emission sites. Here, we demonstrate a geometry-driven strategy to achieve high-current-density field emission from vertically oriented MXene film edge emitters. By systematically controlling the film height and inter-electrode gap, the optimized emitter achieves a current density of 5020 mA cm–2 at 1520 V, which is more than an order of magnitude higher than the values reported for previous MXene field emitters. Enhanced performance is not governed by the field enhancement factor alone. Instead, it is enabled by the balance between sufficient local field enhancement and a large effective emission area. Experimental Fowler–Nordheim analysis, emission pattern imaging, and the screening-corrected field-enhancement model indicate that excessive field concentration can promote edge-localized emission and reduce the effective emission area, whereas the optimized geometry enables distributed edge emission with improved stability. These findings establish edge-geometry engineering as a design principle for transforming two-dimensional MXene films into high-current-density cold cathodes for vacuum nanoelectronics.

title: Peptide–DNA Hybrid Selection for Chemical Functionality Recognition across Diverse Material Interfaces
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Sequence-defined affinity ligands are powerful tools for molecular recognition, yet their selection has largely focused on defined molecular targets rather than shared chemical functionalities. Extending sequence-based recognition to a chemical moiety presents a distinct challenge because the same functionality must be recognized across structurally and chemically diverse molecular and material contexts. Here, we demonstrate that in vitro selection of peptide–DNA hybrids can generate an affinity ligand that recognizes a shared chemical functionality across distinct molecular and material interfaces. Using carboxylates as a model functionality, we selected a peptide–DNA hybrid library against a carboxylated material surface and identified R8rank1, whose enhanced binding depended on the selected DNA sequence functioning within the peptide–DNA hybrid architecture. R8rank1 hybrid preferentially recognized carboxylate-containing polymers with distinct molecular backbones over polymers bearing other functionalities, including an anionic sulfonate-containing polymer, and retained its recognition behavior across chemically distinct gold and silica nanoparticle interfaces presenting surface carboxylates. Fluorescently labeled R8rank1 further distinguished carboxylated from hydroxylated silica nanoparticles with an approximately eightfold difference in fluorescence and exhibited an apparent Kd of approximately 390 nM for the carboxylated surface, whereas the two surfaces were not significantly differentiated by zeta-potential measurements. This affinity-based readout provides chemical-functionality information complementary to conventional surface charge characterization. These findings extend sequence-based affinity selection from defined molecular targets to shared chemical functionalities and establish peptide–DNA hybrids as a selectable molecular recognition platform for identifying chemical functionalities across diverse material interfaces.

title: Electrode-Side Catalytic Regulation Directs Electrolyte Decomposition for Stable Silicon Anodes
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The electrochemical stability of silicon anodes is critically influenced by the initial decomposition pathways of fluorine-containing electrolyte species, which dictate the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) composition and stability. However, existing strategies primarily rely on electrolyte fluorination or artificial interphases to indirectly regulate SEI chemistry, whereas precise electrode-side regulation of fluorine-containing electrolyte decomposition remains challenging. Herein, a binder-free Co SACs-Si-N/C electrode is developed to direct interfacial reactions through single-atom catalysis. Atomically dispersed Co-N4 sites selectively strengthen PF6– adsorption, modulate the interfacial electronic structure, and steer fluorine-containing electrolyte species toward preferential inorganic decomposition, thereby constructing a compact LiF-rich SEI that suppresses parasitic reactions and stabilizes the silicon/electrolyte interface. As a result, the Co SACs-Si-N/C electrode delivers a reversible capacity of 1128.8 mAh g–1 after 1200 cycles at 1.0 A g–1, while lithium cobalt oxide pouch cells further demonstrate their practical applicability. Machine learning established a quantitative correlation between electrochemical characterization parameters and performance evolution. This work reveals the critical role of electrode-regulated interfacial reaction pathways in governing SEI evolution and provides a catalytic strategy for developing durable silicon-based anodes.

title: Boosting Photocatalytic Performance via Electron Transfer Regulation in Biocomponent Hybrid Heterojunctions
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Against the backdrop of global climate change and the energy crisis, developing efficient and sustainable catalytic technologies is crucial for addressing environmental and energy challenges. Compared to traditional heterojunctions, the incorporation of natural biogenic components holds great potential for overcoming bottlenecks such as complex crystal engineering, insufficient stability, and limited selectivity. This review established an electron transfer regulation framework to guide the construction of biocomponent hybrid heterojunctions for superior photocatalysis. We systematically cover various biogenic components and their derivatives, from small molecules, conjugated polymers, and supramolecular assemblies, to three-dimensional networks and crystal frameworks such as metal–organic frameworks and covalent-organic frameworks. Based on in-depth mechanistic analysis, this review demonstrates how these biogenic components modulate band engineering, charge transfer kinetics, substrate utilization, and defect passivation, which collectively achieve sequential optimization across the entire charge-carrier lifecycle—from generation and transport to surface reaction and long-term stability. Importantly, all of these directly linked to enhanced photocatalytic performance in H2 evolution, CO2 reduction, H2O2 generation, and pollutant degradation. In addition to conventional band engineering, novel mechanisms such as exciton behavior modulation and conjugated continuity regulation are discussed. This framework transforms empirical material design into predictable catalysis optimization, aiming to accelerate the development of high-performance biocomponent hybrid heterojunctions.

title: Selenium-Integrated MoO3 Composite Cathode for Rechargeable Magnesium Batteries
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Owing to their high volumetric capacity, potential for low-dendrite metal deposition, and abundance of natural magnesium, rechargeable magnesium batteries (RMBs) have garnered significant interest as potential substitutes for lithium-based systems. Nevertheless, sluggish Mg2+ diffusion and the polyselenide shuttle effect in selenium-based cathodes continue to restrict their practicality. In this work, a Se-MoO3 composite cathode was prepared by solvothermal synthesis of a MoSe2 precursor followed by annealing in air. Compact MoSe2 nanosheets were annealed to create an open hierarchical Se-MoO3 architecture composed of vertically oriented nanosheets associated with MoO3 nanoribbons. The Se-MoO3 cathode delivers 312 mAh g–1 at cycle 80 at 200 mA g–1. At 500 mA g–1, the capacity reaches 237 mAh g–1 at cycle 79 and decreases to 76.8 mAh g–1 at cycle 500. Ex situ measurements reveal reversible changes in the Mo and Se chemical states during cycling, supporting the participation of both components in charge storage. Although the close association between the Se-containing phase and MoO3 may influence the electrochemical response, the present data do not directly establish interface-specific polyselenide adsorption or catalytic conversion. Overall, this work emphasizes compositional and architectural modification as a viable approach for enhanced magnesium-ion storage.

title: D-A-D Engineered Electrochromic Coordination Metallopolymers for Smart Windows, Energy Storage, and Wearables
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Electrochromic coordination metallopolymers featuring multi-redox centers and structural versatility offer great potential for smart windows and glazing, yet they are hampered in practical application owing to the intrinsic trade-off between optical modulation and charge storage. Herein, we introduce a benzothiadiazole acceptor to construct a donor–acceptor–donor architecture that enhances intramolecular charge transfer and enables intervalence charge transfer, narrowing the bandgap and improving near-infrared electrochromism and capacitance. The resulting BT-CMP//V2O5 device exhibits large optical contrast (ΔT > 50%), fast switching (1.7/3.8 s), and high coloration efficiency (>300 cm2·C–1), enabling efficient photothermal modulation with an annual energy saving of 155.19 MJ·m–2. The D-A-D architecture facilitates rapid and complete charge separation, endowing the polymer with superior energy storage performance, including a high areal capacitance of 38.24 mF·cm–2. Furthermore, flexible prototypes exhibit EC and energy storage, maintain stable performance after 100 bending cycles. This D-A-D strategy provides a versatile platform to overcome the intrinsic trade-off of electrochromic materials, paving the way for high-performance electrochromic energy storage devices.

title: Quantitative Solvation Scale for Lithium Battery Electrolytes
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Understanding electrolyte solvation is vital for developing advanced lithium batteries, as solvation structures dictate interfacial chemistry and performance. This study evaluates the reliability of conventional 1D NMR techniques (1H, 7Li, 19F, and 13C) for probing lithium solvation. We demonstrate that absolute chemical shifts often correlate poorly with solvating ability, leading to misleading interpretations—a finding cross-validated by FTIR and DOSY. We identify that the change in chemical shift (Δδ) from 13C NMR serves as a robust descriptor, provided that the probe solvent’s solvating ability matches the system. To overcome single-probe limitations, we introduce a multiprobe strategy using ethyl methyl carbonate (EMC), trifluoroethyl methyl carbonate (FEMC), and propylene carbonate (PC). This approach establishes a quantitative solvation scale across weak, intermediate, and strong solvating regimes. The resulting scale shows strong linear correlations with coordination ratios and solvating power, enabling precise linear free-energy relationships. We demonstrate the practical utility of this framework by accurately predicting lithium nitrate solubility and guiding electrolyte design. Ultimately, this work provides a reliable, broadly applicable methodology for advancing next-generation battery electrolytes. Most importantly, this work provides a lithium solvating strength series, offering a highly useful tool for researchers to compare common solvents.

title: Potential-Dependent Hydricities and Bond Dissociation Free Energies of Metal Surface Hydrides
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Recent experimental studies demonstrate that the thermodynamic hydricity of surface-bound intermediates is continuously tunable via electrical polarization. Canonical density functional theory relies on constant-charge models that fail to capture this potential-dependent polarization at the electrified solid-liquid interface. This work implements grand-canonical density functional theory (GC-DFT) to compute the surface hydricity, bond dissociation free energy (BDFE), and acidity of chemisorbed hydrogen across transition metal facets. Assuming an outer-sphere transfer isolates the intrinsic hydrogen-donating capacity of the active site. By explicitly controlling the system Fermi level, we demonstrate that surface hydricity exhibits a universal linear dependence on applied cathodic bias across all evaluated facets. In contrast, the potential dependence of the homolytic BDFE is strictly governed by material identity: platinum maintains a relatively static bond strength, while silver and copper exhibit potential-induced bond stabilization. The computed hydricity slopes for Pt facets quantitatively reproduce the experimentally measured polarization-dependent hydride-transfer sensitivity. Coordination geometry dictates the baseline donor capacity, with lower coordination atop sites on Ag and Cu functioning as significantly stronger hydride donors. Adlayer saturation perturbs the thermodynamic values in a metal-dependent manner, weakening hydride donation on silver but strengthening it on copper. However, at the two coverages examined, it does not substantially alter the voltage sensitivity of the thermodynamic properties. Evaluating voltage-dependent hydricity provides a thermodynamic framework for characterizing the intrinsic hydride- or hydrogen-donating ability of electrified solid-liquid interfaces.

title: Fe-Regulated Sulfidation of Ni-MOF to Construct an Fe-Ni(OH)2/Ni3S2 Heterojunction for Efficient Hydrogen Evolution in Both Acidic and Alkaline Media
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Developing efficient and durable non-precious electrocatalysts for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) in both acidic and alkaline media is a critical challenge. Herein, we report a Fe-regulated sulfidation strategy that converts a Ni-MOF precursor into a Fe-doped Ni(OH)2/Ni3S2 heterojunction catalyst. Fe acts as a kinetic phase regulator that suppresses the complete conversion of Ni(OH)2 into Ni3S2, stabilizing a mixed phase architecture with abundant heterointerfaces and enlarged electrochemically active surface area. The optimized catalyst delivers exceptional HER performance, requiring overpotentials of only 163.3 mV at –10 mA cm−2 in 1 M KOH and 214.3 mV at –100 mA cm−2 in 0.5 M H2SO4, along with outstanding durability (200 h at –500 mA cm−2 in alkaline electrolyte and 100 h at –100 mA cm−2 in acidic electrolyte). Post-stability characterizations reveal pH-dependent reconstruction: under alkaline conditions, the Ni(OH)2 phase partially dissolves while the Ni3S2 framework remains; under acidic conditions, Fe2+ oxidation to Fe3+ forms a protective M-OH-rich oxide layer on Ni3S2. Density functional theory calculations identify Ni as the primary active site, with Fe functioning as an electronic modulator that redistributes electron density toward Ni and optimizes the d-band center. In alkaline media, the cooperative charge effect and upshifted d-band center synergistically promote water dissociation, with OH* desorption identified as the rate-determining step; in acidic media, strong electrostatic attraction from the highly negatively charged Ni sites dominates H* adsorption. This work highlights the pivotal role of heterojunction engineering and phase regulation in designing durable pH-universal HER catalysts.

title: Engineering Ambipolar Charge Transport in Stable Solution-Processed Nanofilms of Electrically Conductive Liquid-Crystalline Anthraquinones
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The realization of ambipolar charge transport with long-term operational and environmental stability of the transport layer is a rarely addressed challenge in organic electronics, especially with respect to solution-processed devices. This study reports the molecular engineering of redox-active liquid-crystalline anthraquinones with triazole and cyanovinylene functional units to stabilize ordered columnar mesophases at room temperature. In addition to high thermal stability, solution-processed nanofilms of these discotic liquid crystals (DLCs) also demonstrate effective charge-extraction from injecting electrodes in diode devices, with their electrical conductivity values among the highest reported for DLC nanofilms (10–4 S/m). Alongside ultra-stable electrical performance over repeated electrical cycling, these devices exhibit long-term stability for up to two years without encapsulation under ambient storage conditions. Balanced ambipolarity is achieved via the fabrication of single-carrier devices where hole and electron mobilities both match at an order of 10–3 cm2/Vs. Being a pioneering report dedicated to detailed electrical conductivity studies and ambient stability of solution-processed ambipolar DLC films, the present work enriches the scope of practical DLC-based electronic devices from the fundamental viewpoint of molecular design.

title: Dielectric Mie-Resonant Metasurface Integrated ATR Chip for Spectrally Tunable Surface-Enhanced Infrared Spectroscopy in Aqueous Media
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy provides label-free molecular fingerprints but often lacks sensitivity for trace analysis in aqueous media. Surface-enhanced infrared absorption (SEIRA) spectroscopy amplifies vibrational signals near nanostructured surfaces, yet conventional SEIRA platforms typically require sample drying, preconcentration, or noble metal substrates. Here, we introduce a monolithic all-silicon chip that integrates dielectric Mie-resonant micropillar arrays onto a microattenuated total reflection (µ-ATR) element using a complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS)-compatible fabrication process. This µ-ATR SEIRA (µ-SEIRA) chip enables SEIRA directly in bulk aqueous media without sample drying, preconcentration, or noble metals. The µ-SEIRA chip provides spectrally tunable field enhancement, achieving a limit of detection (LOD) of 0.57 mM for aqueous sodium acetate, a 3.6-fold improvement over a flat silicon reference. Resonance tuning via the micropillar array geometry enables selective enhancement of specific vibrational bands, as demonstrated by the preferential enhancement of the Amide II band (∼1550 cm–1) over the Amide I band (∼1650 cm–1) in bovine serum albumin. The µ-SEIRA chip is low-cost, scalable, and disposable, reducing cross-contamination and throughput limitations associated with reusable ATR crystals for aqueous sample measurements.

title: Repurposing Grain Boundaries for Graphene Origami Auxetic Metamaterials with Enhanced Fatigue Resistance
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Graphene represents the pinnacle of intrinsic material strength, yet it remains functionally limited by a lack of plasticity and severe degradation in mechanical performance associated with porosity-driven upscaling. Although graphene origami (GOri) offers a deterministic alternative to porous networks, its realization has been restricted to chemically functionalized, metastable frameworks. Here, we demonstrate a computational design strategy that repurposes grain boundaries (GBs) observed in large-scale chemical vapor deposited (CVD) graphene as topological precursors for stable GOri structures. Using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, we show that periodic pentagon–heptagon (5–7) ring arrays within the tilted GBs can facilitate out-of-plane corrugations of the graphene domains, mimicking macroscopic folding creases without chemical modification. Our study also shows that the mechanical response of the proposed structure is highly tunable via linear grain size (µ) and dimensionless aspect ratio (α), enabling a wide range of control over tensile strength, elastic modulus, and negative Poisson’s ratio (NPR), reaching –3.77. Furthermore, the developed GB-GOri architecture achieves a 20% enhancement in fatigue strength and a fatigue life exceeding 150% of that of functionalized counterparts through pseudo-plastic deformation. Effectively, this GB-assisted defect engineering promotes stable crack growth and provides proof-of-concept for the future experimental fabrication of graphene-based auxetic metamaterials.

title: Linker Steric Hindrance-Induced Defect Engineering Enables Oxygen Vacancy-Rich MOFs for Pollutant Degradation
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The widespread contamination of water by emerging contaminants (ECs) demands the development of efficient remediation technologies. Although advanced oxidation processes reliant on reactive oxygen species (ROS) show promise, they typically depend on energy- or reagent-intensive activation methods. Here, we introduce a linker steric hindrance-induced defect engineering (LSH-DE) strategy for metal–organic frameworks, which enables catalytic ROS generation using molecular oxygen (O2) as a benign terminal oxidant at ambient temperature and pressure. By systematically modulating the steric bulk of organic linkers, we precisely create missing-linker defects and direct the formation of oxygen vacancy (Vo) in robust Ce-UiO-66 during a rapid 15 min synthesis. Spectroscopic and computational analyses confirm that these oxygen vacancies promote O2 adsorption and activation to yield superoxide radicals (•O2–). The optimized catalyst, Ce-UiO-66-(CH3)2, demonstrates superior activity in degrading ubiquitous ECs without requiring external energy inputs or chemical mediators. Furthermore, integration of Ce-UiO-66-(CH3)2 into a membrane-based recirculating flow-through system enabled sustained water treatment, maintaining >90% BPA removal over 48 h with a high water permeance of 101.5 L m–2 h–1 bar–1. This work presents a general and sustainable approach for designing catalytic defects in MOFs, advancing the development of green, next-generation water purification technologies.

title: Mapping the Slow Propagation of Disorder across a Photoreceptor’s Tertiary Structure with Time-Resolved Crystallography
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Order–disorder transitions allow many proteins to shift between compact and flexible/unfolded states, thereby acting as structural switches that regulate catalysis, signaling, recognition, and allostery. We applied time-resolved serial oscillation crystallography to establish the structural kinetics of the light-triggered order–disorder transition of an animal-like cryptochrome as a six-second-long molecular movie with near-atomic all-residue spatial resolution and millisecond temporal resolution. Our 29 structural snapshots mapped the propagation of disorder across the tertiary structure motifs of a cryptochrome’s C-terminal region, triggered by a single broken D321–R492 salt bridge. The order–disorder transition followed a nucleation-propagation mechanism reminiscent of helix–coil dynamics and proceeded over up to five seconds, with regions distal to the D321–R492 trigger initially undergoing slow zero-order disordering before switching to first-order unfolding kinetics. Our per-residue density analysis provides a detailed structural-kinetic basis for understanding how order–disorder transitions emerge through directional propagation across protein tertiary structures, as occurring in signaling and many other biological systems.

title: Electron-Catalyzed Supramolecular Assembly with High Efficiency, Robustness, and Versatility
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Although catalysis is widely exploited by nature to orchestrate noncovalent supramolecular assembly and build up complex living systems, its utilization in synthetic chemistry has conventionally been limited to accelerating covalent reactions. Consequently, the development of artificial systems for catalytic assembly remains a formidable and largely unexplored challenge. Here, we present a rationally designed strategy of electron-catalyzed supramolecular assembly, wherein the electron acts as an efficient, robust, and versatile catalyst to accelerate the formation of a donor–acceptor complex. Optimization of the elementary steps and intermediate stability yields an efficient catalytic cycle, furnishing the process with both a high turnover number and operational robustness in open air. Furthermore, the electron catalysis can be readily triggered by diverse external stimuli─including electricity, light, and mechanical force─enabling precise spatiotemporal control over the assembly process and near-quantitative synthesis of supramolecular complexes. Collectively, this work establishes a well-elucidated strategy of catalytic assembly with remarkable practicality, advancing the frontiers of noncovalent synthetic chemistry.

title: Role of (Co)substrate Coordination to Iron in Activating Its Two-Electron Reduction of Dioxygen: Mechanism of Pterin Activation in Tryptophan Hydroxylase
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Many O2-activating mononuclear nonheme iron enzymes require substrate or cofactor/cosubstrate coordination to iron to form the key peroxy-bridged intermediate necessary for catalysis with no net change in the iron redox state. The role of (co)substrate coordination, however, remained unclear. Here, we leverage a pterin-dependent enzyme, tryptophan hydroxylase, for which cosubstrate (pterin) coordination can be experimentally controlled by the absence and presence of substrate, to explicitly determine the role of pterin coordination in O2 binding and peroxo formation. EPR, absorption, circular dichroism, and magnetic circular dichroism spectroscopies on the {FeNO}7 analog of the unobservable {FeO2}8 intermediate without and with pterin coordination demonstrate that pterin coordination induces new absorption bands and enhances NO affinity by 3.6 kcal mol–1 at 277 K. These new bands are pterin-to-iron ligand-to-metal charge-transfer transitions that compensate the electron donation from iron to NO upon NO binding. Extension of our findings on {FeNO}7 to {FeO2}8 evidences that pterin coordination stabilizes O2 binding and facilitates the two-electron transfer from pterin to {FeO2}8 to reduce the transition-state barrier for peroxo formation by 12.7 kcal mol–1, corresponding to a 1010 increase in reaction rate. The electron transfer pathways established herein underscore a unified mechanism for the pterin-dependent, α-ketoglutarate-dependent, extradiol, and intradiol dioxygenase families of mononuclear nonheme iron enzymes through which (co)substrate coordination enhances O2 binding via one-electron transfer within {FeO2}8 and two-electron donation from the (co)substrate (one to bound O2 and one to iron) to generate the peroxo species with no net redox change on the iron.

title: A Crystalline LaCl3 Reinforced Amorphous Oxyhalide Electrolyte for Thermally Stable All-Solid-State Batteries
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract All-solid-state batteries (ASSBs) are a promising next-generation energy storage technology, but their development is often constrained by the thermal instability and high cost of solid-state electrolytes (SSEs). Amorphous oxyhalide electrolytes, while mechanically deformable, are particularly susceptible to thermal degradation. Here, we report a novel and cost-effective composite SSE fabricated by embedding LaCl3 nanocrystals within an amorphous Li–Al–O–Cl (LAOC) matrix. This unique architecture synergistically combines the high ionic conductivity of the amorphous phase with the enhanced thermal and mechanical robustness imparted by the crystalline phase. The resulting Li–La–Al–O–Cl electrolyte achieves a high room-temperature ionic conductivity exceeding 1 mS cm–1 and demonstrates exceptional thermal stability, remaining a solid powder at 150 °C, a temperature at which the baseline LAOC melts. This enhanced thermal and thermo-mechanical integrity, combined with excellent deformability, enables superior interfacial contact and stability with cathodes. The Li–La–Al–O–Cl-based ASSBs maintain stable operation at 80 °C, in stark contrast to the rapid failure of LAOC-based cells. This strategy of reinforcing a soft amorphous matrix with a rigid crystalline offers a new pathway for designing thermally robust, high-performance, and commercially viable SSEs.

title: Molecular Mechanophores Based on Stress-Enhanced Exciton Transition between Phosphorescent Probes and Polymer Matrix
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Mechanophores provide an in situ and remote tool for quantifying invisible stress in polymers by photonic signals, offering distinct advantages for stress distribution analysis of large-area surfaces and instrument-free stress observation. However, achieving an ideal mechanophore that integrates with sensitive, reversible, and molecular-level stress sensing is attractive yet challenging. Here, we report practical guidance for developing ideal mechanophores that promote the molecular probe’s exciton transition for room-temperature phosphorescence (RTP) under stress, through the “assisted lowest triplet (T1) state” of the adjacent polymer chain.
